articles.title: France school students blockade hundreds of schools in protests
articles.summary: More than 400 people, mainly minors, were arrested on Tuesday, the country's interior minister says.
articles.body:
More than 400 people, most of them children, were arrested in France on Tuesday during a wave of school protests across the country.

The country's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told broadcaster BFMTV that 440 people in total had been detained, while 48 law enforcement members had been injured.

Students are demonstrating over issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. France's education ministry said 400 schools were impacted by protests or disruptions on Tuesday.

The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.

The protests on Tuesday came the same day as professionals from public sectors - including teachers and firefighters - also demonstrated against planned budget cuts in France.

articles.title: How cold is too cold for dogs? Vets explain what to know about pet winter safety
articles.summary: Dogs can get frostbite and hypothermia, too. Vets explain how to keep them warm and protect their paws, plus what to know about pet-safe ice melt.
articles.body: Once the temperature starts steadily dropping, I don’t think about getting my parka and snow boots out of storage — I immediately begin worrying about keeping my dog warm and safe when we go outside. Like people, dogs are at risk for frostbite and hypothermia if they’re exposed to the cold for too long. Slipping on ice, frozen paws and exposure to chemical de-icers are concerns for pet parents, too. To make the winter more comfortable for your dog, I talked to two veterinarians about how to protect them from chilly, snowy weather. Vets also broke down their top winter safety tips, including what to do if your pet comes into contact with dangerous substances like ice melt, rock salt and antifreeze. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best winter gear for dogs There’s two main components to dog winter safety: keeping pups warm and protecting their paws. You’ll need different gear to address each area — for example, coats help dogs retain body heat, while booties can prevent dogs from slipping on ice and stepping in toxic salt. The items I recommend in this article cover various needs and meet veterinarians’ shopping guidance. They include highly rated items and those NBC Selected pet parents use themselves. Experts also explain the purpose behind each product and when to use it. How to keep dogs warm in the winter Dog coats, jackets and sweaters aren’t just a fashion statement — the right one helps keep your pet warm, similar to humans. But not all dogs need the extra winter layer, says Dr. Hannah Hart, a veterinarian at Chewy. (Ed’s note: The inclusion of products sold by Chewy in this article was made independently of Hart). It depends on a dog’s size, coat length, health status, activity level and time spent outside. Smaller dogs and/or those with short fur coats, like chihuahuas and greyhounds, for example, often benefit most from outerwear, as do dogs with thin skin, like those that are older or have certain medical conditions, including Cushing’s disease, says Hart. If your dog is highly active and produces a lot of body heat while running and playing, they may not need a coat. However, a thin, water-resistant layer can be helpful for even the largest, thickest-coated dogs to keep them dry during weather like snow and freezing rain, says Dr. Aly Cohen, an extension veterinarian for the Cornell Riney Canine Health Center. It’s also important to remember that adding extra layers is most important for longer trips outside compared to short excursions, like getting from your home to a car parked nearby. Below are some of our favorite winter coats for dogs. Best jacket This jacket is designed with everything veterinarians recommend looking for while shopping for dogs’ winter outerwear. It has a water-resistant exterior to keep your pet dry, as well as insulation and a fleece lining to keep them warm. Plus, the jacket is reflective, which Hart says is an important safety feature. Daylight hours are shorter in the winter, so you’ll likely have to take your dog outside in low light conditions — reflective apparel ensures that cars, bicyclists and other people see your pup. Spark Paws’ jacket easily snaps on and off with double-breasted buttons so you can adjust its fit. There’s also a small zippered pocket to store essentials, and if you put a harness underneath the jacket, you can attach a leash to it via a zipper hole. It offers full coverage across the back, chest and stomach, too. Best coat Carhartt’s coat doesn’t have as much chest and stomach coverage as the one from Spark Paws’, but it’s still warm since it’s insulated and has a quilted liner. You also may find it easier to put on your pet, especially if they’re squirmy. Rather than buttons, the coat’s adjustable Velcro straps wrap around your dog’s stomach and chest. Carhartt’s coat is made from a water-repellent canvas exterior that also protects them from wind, and there’s pockets on its sides for essentials, as well as a plush collar. It’s important to note that this coat doesn’t have a hole for harness access or leash attachment points. Best fleece A fleece like this one is ideal for days when it’s chilly enough for your dog to need an extra layer, but not cold enough for their heavy coat. It’s also great for layering — I often put my dog’s fleece under her rain jacket in the fall to keep her extra warm. Gooby’s fleece is double-sided, so it’s soft against your dog’s body as well as on the exterior, and there’s a dual D-ring leash attachment. It also has a high collar to protect your pet’s neck. The vest’s half zipper creates a large opening to pull the fleece over your dog’s head. It offers full coverage across the back, chest and stomach. Best snow suit If you live in an area that tends to get a lot of snow, or you plan to visit one this winter, your pup might need more protection than a standard coat offers. A full-body snow suit like this one keeps dogs warm and prevents snowball buildup in their fur — despite its extra coverage, however, it won’t restrict their movement. Canada Pooch’s snow suit has a water-resistant shell and thermal foil lining to help your dog retain heat, as well as a high funnel neck with adjustable toggles to keep wind and wetness out. The pant hem on each leg is also adjustable thanks to button snaps. There’s a side zipper closure to easily get the snow suit on and off your dog. Best snood “Snoods are another helpful winter gear item for dogs,” says Hart. “They’re a wraparound head covering that goes over the ears to protect them from frostbite, as the thin ear flaps can lose heat easily in cold weather.” Zoni Pets’ Happy Hoodie is an example of a snood made from soft, stretchy, thick, double-ply fabric. Beyond being a warm winter accessory, it also calms and comforts pets when they’re anxious, according to the brand. The Happy Hoodie applies gentle compression around dogs’ ears, which reduces noise during grooming, fireworks, thunder, car rides and vet visits, and has a swaddling effect. This machine-washable snood comes in four sizes — a more snug fit is better at reducing noise and stress compared to a less snug fit. How to protect dogs’ paws in the winter Dogs’ paws are particularly vulnerable to the cold, wet weather since they can get frostbite, and their paw pads can become dry, cracked and irritated after repeat exposure to winter conditions. Chemical de-icers, like the ice melt and rock salt you typically see on sidewalks and in parking lots, is also a major concern. It’s toxic to dogs if ingested, whether they lick it off the ground or from their paws after stepping in it, says Hart. To protect dogs’ paws in the winter, the vets I spoke to recommend using booties, which put a barrier between the ground and your pup’s feet. However, not all dogs tolerate booties, and it can be challenging to find a pair that fits properly, especially for small breeds. If booties don’t work for your pet, clean their paws with wipes immediately after a trip outside, and apply protective paw balm to prevent dryness and cracks. Best dog booties Finding a pair of booties that fits your dog and that they tolerate might take some trial-and-error since each pair is sized differently. Try introducing them indoors before venturing outside, and do some focused training, too, says Cohen — put them on your pet and give them treats for walking in them, not biting at them and not pulling them off. PawZ Rubber Dog Boots come in a pack of 12, so you get three sets of four. They’re essentially grippy socks that offer traction to prevent your pet from slipping on slick surfaces, like ice-covered pavement. The water-resistant boots also keep dogs’ feet warm and dry in the snowy weather, plus reduce the risk of paw pad injuries from ice and exposure to de-icers. Your dog can wear each set of boots multiple times before they begin to wear down and form holes, according to the brand — at that point, toss the old pair and use a new one. Best dog booties with traction Older dogs and those with mobility issues tend to need extra support on snow and ice in the winter, says Hart, which boots like these can help with. Compared to the option from PawZ above, Ruffwear’s boots have a thicker, more grippy, lug-like outsole, giving your pet maximum stability. Their wide opening helps you slip them over dogs’ paws, and the adjustable hook-and-loop cinch closure at the ankle keeps them in place. The boots are made with a flexible, breathable, padded mesh lining to prevent chaffing, rubbing and stiff walking, according to the brand. Ruffwear sells these booties in a pack of two, so you’ll need to buy two sets for all four paws — dogs often have wider front paws and narrower rear paws, so measure both before purchasing in case you need two sizes. Whether you’re preventing your dog’s paw pads from becoming dry or healing existing irritation, Musher’s Secret wax will do the trick. It’s made from a blend of soothing, natural, non-toxic ingredients like waxes and oils with vitamin E, and it’s lick-safe. The paw wax also dries quickly and is non-staining, so you don’t have to worry about it getting on surfaces in your home. You can apply the wax before trips outside to create a breathable, protective barrier over dogs’ paws, or afterward as a moisturizer. The wax is suitable for dogs’ noses, elbows and other chapped areas of skin on their body as well. I go through about one pack of Earth Rated’s Pet Wipes a month with my dog since I use them to clean her paws, legs, stomach and chest after walks or trips to the park. I’m sure I’ll rely on them even more this winter once we’re dealing with dirty snow and salt. The textured wipes effectively remove grime, and since they’re thick and durable, they never tear during use, in my experience. They’re also made with ingredients like aloe, shea butter, chamomile and cucumber, making them gentle and non-drying. I appreciate that the wipes’ come in a resealable container, which prevents them from drying out between uses. They’re always moist enough when I need them, but not soaking wet or drippy. Why is ice melt dangerous for dogs? In the winter, you’ll often see ice melt and rock salt covering pavement roads, driveways, parking lots and sidewalks. These chemical substances, which look like white, clear or blue crystals, are typically made with sodium chloride (salt) and other minerals. They help melt ice even in sub-freezing temperatures, as well as prevent new ice from forming. While ice melt and rock salt can make surfaces safer to walk on in the winter, they’re dangerous for dogs to ingest, just like regular table salt is, says Hart. If dogs lick too much of either substance from the ground or their paws, it can cause salt poisoning, dehydration and kidney issues, which can appear as symptoms like vomiting, diarrhea, low energy, shaking or seizures, drooling and disorientation, says Hart. It can also be abrasive to the paws and cause redness, irritation and excessive licking, which can lead to open sores and skin infections. Is pet-safe ice melt actually pet-safe? Some ice melt and rock salt says “pet-safe” on its label, which usually means it’s free from sodium chloride (salt) and instead made with chemicals like urea and magnesium chloride. Cohen recommends using these pet-safe options at home when possible, although they’re not completely benign. “Pet-safe usually means the product is less harmful than a traditional de-icer, but pet-safe doesn’t mean zero risk,” she says. “They’re just less irritating, but could still cause mild irritation, though some pets may be more sensitive than others. Dogs should still be prevented from trying to lick their paws after contact or prolonged exposure.” Below is an example of pet-safe rock salt. What to do if your dog is exposed to ice melt Wearing booties every time they go outside is the only way for your dog to completely avoid contact with rock salt and/or ice melt in the winter. If they don’t tolerate booties, vets recommend immediately cleaning their paws when they come inside and applying a healing paw balm. Cohen also suggests cleaning your dog’s legs, stomach and chest, especially if their body is low to the ground, to decrease the amount of time the chemicals are in contact with their skin and reduce the risk of ingestion. For minor rock salt and/or ice melt exposures, clean your dogs’ feet with standard paw wipes or a soft cloth with lukewarm water. For larger skin exposures, Hart recommends washing your pet’s paws with gentle dish soap like Dawn Original, rinsing with lukewarm water and drying thoroughly. Also, be sure to monitor for injuries like redness, crackness, limp paws and discomfort, says Cohen. Contact your vet if you notice anything unusual. If you’re worried about your dog licking rock salt and/or ice melt off the ground while they’re outside, Hart recommends keeping them on a shorter leash to reduce their ability to wander off unsupervised. Also, do some training. “Positively reinforce ignoring the salt on the ground with high-value treats and their favorite toys, which also distracts them, and praise and reward them for leaving the salt alone,” she says. Vet-approved dog winter safety tips: Do’s and don’ts Here are a few additional winter safety tips vets say pet owners should know. Do your longest walk in the middle of the day, says Hart. That’s when the temperature is typically the highest and light levels are the brightest, making for more comfortable conditions. If it’s too cold to walk your dog outside, some pet-friendly stores like Lowe’s and Home Depot may allow you to walk your dog inside, says Hart. This activity is mentally stimulating and lets your pet get some exercise in.Never leave your dog in the car with the heat off, says Hart. The inside of your car can get cold quickly.To prepare for a snowstorm and winter-related power outages, always keep at least five days worth of extra dog food, bottled water and medications (prescriptions and flea/tick preventatives) at home, says Hart.Make sure your dog wears a collar with an ID tag that has your contact information, and is microchipped. (Double check that the microchip is registered to you with your contact information, too. Your vet can help with this.) Dogs who are lost in the winter often have a harder time finding their way home due to snow, ice and cold temperatures, says Hart. Microchips and collars with identifying information help people quickly alert the dog’s family.In addition to rock salt and ice melt, beware of your dog’s exposure to antifreeze, a coolant for vehicles’ engines. It’s extremely toxic and deadly to pets if ingested, so use extreme caution if you store it in your garage and immediately clean it up if it spills. Also, be careful about what your dog sniffs, licks and steps in if you walk them near autobody shops, gas stations and car washes.Keep your dog away from indoor hazards like space heaters, wood stoves and fireplaces to ensure they don’t accidentally burn themselves, says Cohen. Meet our veterinary experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure that all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and with no undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Aly Cohen is an extension veterinarian for the Cornell Riney Canine Health Center and a clinical instructor for the Cornell Maddie’s Shelter Medicine Program.Dr. Hannah Hart is a veterinarian at Chewy. (Ed’s note: The inclusion of products sold by Chewy in this article was made independently of Hart). Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who has written about pet products for over five years. I’ve covered topics like how to keep dogs cool in the summer, flea treatments, cat food, cat toys, dog training treats and cat travel carriers. I’m also a pet parent myself — I have a dog, two cats and a turtle. I’ve volunteered at animal shelters for over a decade as well, and I’m a former dog walker. To write this article, I interviewed two veterinarians about dog winter safety. Using their guidance, as well as my own knowledge as a pet owner, I recommended related cold weather gear. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Hiperbárica: tecnologia que une medicina, recuperação e cuidado indivi | G1
articles.standfirst: Tratamento com oxigênio pressurizado desperta interesse nas áreas médica, esportiva e estética; em São Carlos, clínica aposta em uma experiência acolhedora para os pacientes
articles.summary: Tratamento com oxigênio pressurizado desperta interesse nas áreas médica, esportiva e estética; em São Carlos, clínica aposta em uma experiência acolhedora para os pacientes
articles.body:
Hiperbárica: tecnologia que une medicina, recuperação e cuidado individualizado — Foto: Crédito: Divulgação

Uma tecnologia que envolve ciência, pressão e oxigênio, mas que, para quem está dentro da câmara, pode representar muito mais do que um procedimento. A oxigenoterapia hiperbárica vem ganhando espaço como recurso complementar em diferentes áreas da medicina e despertando a atenção de pacientes que buscam alternativas para recuperação e cuidados com o organismo.

Em São Carlos, a chegada da OxyLife São Carlos acompanha esse movimento e traz à cidade uma proposta que combina tecnologia e, principalmente, atenção à experiência de cada paciente.

A oxigenoterapia hiperbárica, conhecida como OHB, consiste na administração de oxigênio em alta concentração em um ambiente com pressão superior à atmosférica. Essa combinação aumenta significativamente a quantidade de oxigênio dissolvido no plasma sanguíneo, favorecendo sua disponibilidade para determinados tecidos, normalmente respiramos 20% de oxigênio em ar ambiente, e durante essa experiência, vamos respirar em oxigênio em 100% durante o procedimento, que tem duração média de 90 minutos.

O tratamento possui indicações médicas reconhecidas para diferentes condições, incluindo algumas feridas de difícil cicatrização, queimaduras, determinadas infecções, lesões por esmagamento, comprometimento de enxertos e retalhos, osteomielite e lesões relacionadas à radioterapia.

Mais oxigênio, mais possibilidades terapêuticas

O oxigênio participa de processos fundamentais para o funcionamento celular e para a reparação dos tecidos.

Entre os mecanismos estudados estão a atividade de fibroblastos, a produção de colágeno, a formação de novos vasos sanguíneos e a modulação de determinados processos inflamatórios.

Se existe uma área em que a recuperação é constantemente colocada à prova, é o esporte.

Treinos intensos, competições, traumas e sobrecarga física fazem parte da rotina de atletas profissionais e amadores. Por isso, pesquisadores vêm estudando o papel da oxigenoterapia hiperbárica na recuperação após exercícios e lesões.

Estudos recentes apontam resultados promissores em alguns marcadores relacionados à recuperação muscular. Pesquisas também observaram redução do lactato após períodos de recuperação em atletas.

Ao mesmo tempo, a ciência mostra que os resultados não são uniformes para todos os objetivos. A hiperbárica não deve ser apresentada como uma forma universal de acelerar a recuperação ou eliminar dores musculares.

A tendência é que a terapia seja utilizada como recurso complementar, dentro de uma estratégia que pode envolver avaliação médica, fisioterapia, treinamento adequado, sono, alimentação e controle de carga.

E o que a hiperbárica tem a ver com estética?

A relação entre oxigenação, reparação dos tecidos e produção de colágeno também despertou o interesse da medicina estética.

Pesquisas vêm avaliando a utilização da oxigenoterapia hiperbárica principalmente em processos de recuperação após determinados procedimentos. Alguns estudos apontam resultados positivos em parâmetros relacionados à cicatrização.

Há também pesquisas investigando possíveis efeitos sobre colágeno e elastina.

Mas existe uma diferença importante entre potencial terapêutico e promessa estética.

Ainda não existem evidências suficientes para tratar a hiperbárica como uma solução isolada para rejuvenescimento ou como substituta de procedimentos estéticos convencionais. Seu uso deve ser avaliado de acordo com o objetivo e as condições de cada paciente.

Uma experiência que começa antes da sessão

Se a tecnologia é parte importante do tratamento, a experiência do paciente também merece atenção.

Esse é um dos principais pontos trabalhados pela OxyLife São Carlos: o cuidado começa no momento em que o paciente chega à clínica.

Para muitas pessoas, entrar em uma câmara hiperbárica é uma experiência completamente nova. Algumas chegam com dúvidas, outras com receio de não saber como será o procedimento.

Por isso, um acolhimento bem realizado pode fazer diferença.

Explicar o que acontecerá durante a sessão, ouvir as dúvidas, acompanhar o paciente e proporcionar um ambiente confortável são atitudes que ajudam a tornar a experiência mais leve e favorecem a confiança e a adesão ao tratamento.

Na prática, a proposta da OxyLife é que o paciente não seja tratado apenas como alguém que está realizando uma sessão, mas como uma pessoa que precisa ser orientada e acompanhada durante todo o processo.

Uma curiosidade: não é simplesmente respirar oxigênio

Uma das dúvidas mais comuns de quem nunca teve contato com a terapia é imaginar que a hiperbárica seja apenas uma forma de receber mais oxigênio.

O diferencial está justamente na combinação entre oxigênio e pressão elevada.

Dentro da câmara, a pressão é aumentada de maneira controlada. Isso permite que uma quantidade maior de oxigênio seja dissolvida no plasma sanguíneo e transportada pelo organismo.

Durante o procedimento, o paciente pode sentir uma sensação de pressão nos ouvidos, semelhante à experimentada durante a decolagem ou aterrissagem de um avião. A equipe orienta o paciente sobre como realizar a equalização dessa pressão.

Outra curiosidade: cada tratamento pode ser diferente

Não existe necessariamente um protocolo único para todas as pessoas.

A indicação, o número de sessões, a duração e os parâmetros utilizados dependem da finalidade do tratamento e da avaliação profissional.

Por isso, antes de iniciar um protocolo, é fundamental compreender qual é o objetivo e se existe indicação para aquele paciente.

Essa individualização também ajuda a estabelecer expectativas mais realistas.

A nova fase da medicina hiperbárica em São Carlos

A chegada da OxyLife São Carlos representa mais uma opção para quem busca acesso à tecnologia hiperbárica na cidade.

Mas, além da estrutura e dos equipamentos, a clínica aposta em um conceito simples: cuidar da pessoa durante o tratamento é tão importante quanto oferecer a tecnologia adequada.

Para quem pratica esportes, isso pode significar encontrar um ambiente preparado para integrar a terapia à rotina de recuperação.

Para pacientes que chegam por indicação médica, pode representar uma experiência mais tranquila durante um tratamento que, muitas vezes, já acontece em um momento delicado.

E, para quem busca cuidados relacionados à estética e à recuperação dos tecidos, significa encontrar informação e orientação antes de criar expectativas.

A medicina hiperbárica continua sendo objeto de pesquisas e novas descobertas. Algumas aplicações já possuem indicações consolidadas, enquanto outras continuam sendo estudadas.

O caminho mais seguro é evitar promessas milagrosas e compreender a terapia dentro de suas reais possibilidades.

Em São Carlos, a OxyLife aposta justamente nessa combinação: tecnologia, conhecimento e acolhimento.

Porque, no fim das contas, uma experiência de tratamento mais leve começa antes mesmo de a câmara ser pressurizada.

O cuidado começa no acolhimento. A tecnologia faz parte do caminho. E cada paciente tem sua própria jornada.

articles.title: Chuva destrói parte da estrutura de propriedade do cantor Zé Neto | G1
articles.standfirst: A forte chuva ocorreu na noite de segunda-feira (28) em Ipiguá (SP) e deixou diversos moradores sem energia elétrica.
articles.summary: Uma forte chuva na noite de segunda-feira (28), em Ipiguá (SP), afetou diversas zonas da cidade incluindo a área rural onde uma propriedade do cantor Zé Neto.
articles.body:
A forte chuva registrada na noite de segunda-feira (28) em Ipiguá (SP) causou danos a uma propriedade rural do cantor sertanejo Zé Neto, da cupla com Cristiano.

Um vídeo recebido pela produção da TV TEM mostra que parte da estrutura do local desabou com a força do vento e da água. Assista ao vídeo acima. O g1 fez contato com a assessoria de imprensa do artista para tentar mais informações sobre prejuízos e transtornos, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Estrutura da propriedade do cantor Zé Neto foi danificada durante chuva em Ipiguá (SP) — Foto: Reprodução / WhatsApp

A tempestade durou cerca de 20 minutos, mas deixou moradores sem energia elétrica em algumas regiões da cidade. No total, 4.253 imóveis foram afetados pela interrupção do serviço, segundo informado pela Companhia de Força e Luz Paulista (CPFL).

Alguns vídeos recebidos pela TV TEM mostram que a ventania veio acompanhada de raios e trovões. Veja abaixo.

Em uma fazenda, o vento derrubou um poste e danificou a rede de alta tensão. Em outros pontos, também houve registro de postes que não resistiram às consequências do mau tempo.

Vento derruba poste e danifica rede de alta tensão em Ipiguá (SP) — Foto: TV TEM / Rodrigo Carraro

No Conjunto Habitacional Vida Nova em São José do Rio Preto (SP), que fica próximo a Ipiguá , moradores também foram afetados pela interrupção do serviço de energia. Segundo a população, o problema é recorrente em dias de chuva.

Em nota, a Companhia de Força e Luz Paulista informou que, ao todo, 4.253 imóveis foram afetados em Ipiguá e oito postes de energia caíram. Leia a íntegra abaixo.

Zé Neto e Cristiano — Foto: Thomaz Marostegan - Arquivo

"Em razão das fortes chuvas e rajadas de vento registradas na tarde de 28/09/2026, na região norte de São José do Rio Preto e no município de Ipiguá, a rede da CPFL Paulista sofreu a quebra de oito postes de energia.

A energia recebida pela CERRP é proveniente da rede da CPFL Paulista, por meio de dois pontos de conexão, e posteriormente distribuída aos consumidores atendidos pela CERRP. Por esse motivo, a ocorrência na rede da CPFL prejudicou o fornecimento de energia e os serviços prestados pela CERRP.

As primeiras reclamações foram registradas às 19h12. As equipes da CERRP foram imediatamente acionadas e iniciaram os deslocamentos às 19h15. Diante do elevado número de ocorrências, as equipes de sobreaviso também foram mobilizadas e começaram os atendimentos às 20h05.

Ao todo, 4.253 unidades consumidoras foram afetadas."

articles.title: Morre Azul, produtor e pesquisador da música paraense Edvaldo Souza | G1
articles.standfirst: Edvaldo Souza criou o projeto MúsicaParaense.Org e reuniu acervo dedicado à produção musical do estado; velório ocorre nesta terça-feira (29), em Belém
articles.summary: Morre Azul, produtor cultural Edvaldo Souza, criador do projeto MúsicaParaense.Org e guardião de um acervo histórico com milhares de registros da música do Pará.
articles.body:
Edvaldo Souza, o Azul, produtor cultural, DJ e pesquisador que dedicou mais de 25 anos à música paraense. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Morreu Edvaldo Pinto Pereira de Souza, conhecido como Azul, produtor cultural, DJ e pesquisador que dedicou mais de 25 anos à música paraense. A morte foi comunicada nesta terça-feira (29) pelo curso de Museologia da Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA), onde ele era estudante. O velório será realizado a partir das 15h, no Teatro Margarida Schivasappa, em Belém .

A trajetória de Azul foi marcada pela pesquisa, preservação e divulgação da produção musical do Pará. Em 1998, ele criou o MúsicaParaense.Org, projeto dedicado ao mapeamento de artistas, à pesquisa da musicografia paraense e à circulação de trabalhos de diferentes gêneros.

A iniciativa surgiu do interesse pela música autoral produzida no estado e das possibilidades abertas pela internet para ampliar o alcance desses trabalhos. Com o passar dos anos, o projeto se transformou em um banco de dados e acervo digital da música paraense.

O acervo reunido a partir desse trabalho chegou a mais de 5 mil títulos digitalizados, com registros de diferentes períodos da produção local. O material também se tornou fonte de consulta para pesquisadores interessados em gêneros e movimentos ligados à música produzida no Pará.

Azul também atuou como produtor cultural e produtor executivo. Ao longo da carreira, esteve envolvido em trabalhos com artistas como Joãozinho Gomes, Pio Lobato e Everton MC. Sua atuação ainda passou pela curadoria e pela discotecagem, levando para apresentações públicas parte da pesquisa musical desenvolvida ao longo de décadas.

Em janeiro de 2025, uma apresentação em Belém foi divulgada como uma viagem pela história da música paraense a partir da pesquisa e da discotecagem de Azul. Na ocasião, ele foi apresentado como pesquisador dedicado havia mais de 25 anos à música produzida no estado.

Além da atuação no cenário cultural, Azul era estudante do curso de Museologia da UFPA. Em nota de pesar, a graduação destacou a presença dele na vida acadêmica.

“Durante sua trajetória acadêmica, seu Evaldo destacou-se como um aluno dedicado, comprometido e presente, deixando sua marca entre colegas, professores e servidores do curso”, diz a nota.

Amigos e familiares também publicaram uma homenagem em que o definem como DJ, produtor, produtor musical e guardião de “um dos mais importantes acervos da música paraense”. Na mensagem, eles convidam o público a se despedir e homenagear “sua vida, sua memória e seu legado”.

articles.summary: More than two decades of US military presence in Iraq comes to an end.
articles.body:
The last remaining US troops have left Iraq. The US military was first deployed to Iraq back in 2003 to depose its leader, Saddam Hussein.

articles.title: Retatrutida leva metade dos pacientes com diabetes a sair da obesidade; efeitos colaterais crescem com a dose | G1
articles.standfirst: Publicação do TRIUMPH-2 na Lancet mostra que até 40% dos participantes chegaram a uma glicemia normal e que diarreia, náusea e alterações de sensibilidade na pele aumentam com a dose. O remédio ainda não tem aprovação em nenhum país.
articles.summary: Publicação do TRIUMPH-2 na Lancet mostra que até 40% dos participantes chegaram a uma glicemia normal e que diarreia, náusea e alterações de sensibilidade na pele aumentam com a dose. O remédio ainda não tem aprovação em nenhum país.
articles.body:
Mais da metade dos adultos com diabetes tipo 2 que receberam a dose mais alta da retatrutida deixou de ter obesidade após 80 semanas de tratamento. Até quatro em cada dez participantes chegaram a níveis normais de glicose no sangue.

Os resultados completos do TRIUMPH-2 também detalham os efeitos colaterais do remédio. Um em cada três pacientes da dose mais alta teve diarreia, e 7,3% relataram alterações de sensibilidade na pele. O TRIUMPH-2 é um estudo de fase 3 da farmacêutica Eli Lilly, a última etapa de testes antes do pedido de aprovação.

Os dados foram apresentados nesta terça-feira (29) no congresso anual da Associação Europeia para o Estudo do Diabetes (EASD), em Milão, e publicados ao mesmo tempo na revista científica The Lancet.

A retatrutida é uma injeção semanal da mesma família do Ozempic (semaglutida) e do Mounjaro (tirzepatida).

Esses remédios imitam hormônios produzidos pelo intestino que aumentam a saciedade e ajudam a controlar a glicose. A semaglutida age sobre um desses hormônios, e a tirzepatida, sobre dois. A retatrutida é a primeira a agir também sobre o glucagon, hormônio que faz o organismo gastar mais energia.

A empresa já havia divulgado o resultado principal do estudo em julho: na dose de 12 mg, a perda média foi de 20,8% do peso, cerca de 22,5 kg . A publicação acrescenta agora os resultados por subgrupo, as metas de controle da glicose, o efeito sobre marcadores de risco cardiovascular e o perfil de segurança da molécula.

Os 1.152 participantes começaram o estudo pesando, em média, 106,4 kg, com índice de massa corporal (IMC) de 38,2, o que corresponde à obesidade grau 2.

Entre os que tinham IMC igual ou superior a 35, a dose de 12 mg levou a uma redução média de 23,4% do peso, ou 27,5 kg . Ao fim do tratamento, 59,5% de todos os pacientes que tomaram 12 mg estavam abaixo de 30 de IMC, o limite que define a obesidade.

A perda de peso foi expressiva em todas as doses:

No grupo placebo, que recebeu uma injeção sem o remédio, os participantes perderam 4% do peso.

Segundo Clayton Macedo, doutor em endocrinologia e diretor da Sociedade Brasileira de Endocrinologia e Metabologia (SBEM), o resultado ganha relevância por se tratar de pessoas com diabetes tipo 2.

Nessa população, a resistência à insulina e o uso de outros medicamentos costumam limitar o efeito dos remédios para obesidade. O TRIUMPH-2, afirma o especialista, mostra que perdas muito grandes também são possíveis nesse grupo.

A diferença aparece quando se compara com outro estudo da mesma molécula. No TRIUMPH-1, que avaliou adultos com obesidade ou sobrepeso associados a outras doenças, a dose de 12 mg levou a uma redução média de 28,3%.

O controle da diabetes melhorou junto com o peso. A hemoglobina glicada, exame que mostra a média de açúcar no sangue nos últimos três meses, caiu cerca de 1,5 ponto percentual em todas as doses.

Com as doses mais altas, quase oito em cada dez participantes ficaram abaixo do valor usado para diagnosticar o diabetes, contra um em cada quatro no grupo placebo. Cerca de 40% chegaram a níveis considerados normais.

O investigador principal do estudo, Juan P. Frías, do Los Angeles Institute for Metabolic Research, lembra que a maioria das pessoas com diabetes tipo 2 também tem obesidade. Segundo ele, tratar as duas condições ao mesmo tempo sempre foi um desafio, e resultados nesse patamar podem mudar o que se espera de uma única terapia para esses pacientes.

Além do peso e da glicose, o remédio melhorou exames usados para estimar o risco de doenças do coração. Os números abaixo comparam, em média, os valores ao fim de 80 semanas com os do início do estudo, entre os pacientes que tomaram a dose mais alta:

Triglicerídeos , um tipo de gordura no sangue: ficaram 39,5% mais baixos.

Colesterol não-HDL , que reúne as frações de colesterol que se acumulam nas artérias: ficou 19,6% mais baixo.

Pressão arterial : a máxima caiu 10,8 mmHg, o equivalente a passar de 14 por 9 para cerca de 13 por 9.

Proteína C-reativa , que indica inflamação no organismo: ficou 58,3% mais baixa.

Esses resultados, no entanto, ainda não permitem afirmar que a retatrutida previne infarto, acidente vascular cerebral (AVC) ou doença renal. Segundo Macedo, exames melhores não significam necessariamente menos casos dessas doenças, e só estudos feitos para acompanhar esses eventos podem dar essa resposta. A Lilly conduz pesquisas desse tipo, mas os resultados ainda não foram divulgados.

O artigo da Lancet traz um percentual de perda de peso abaixo do divulgado pela empresa. Os 20,8% vêm da chamada análise de eficácia, que estima o efeito do remédio caso todos os voluntários tivessem seguido o tratamento até o fim, ainda que com ajustes temporários de dose.

A revista também publica a análise por regime de tratamento, que inclui os participantes que abandonaram a medicação de vez. Por esse critério, a perda média na dose de 12 mg é de 18,8%, e 47% dos pacientes perderam ao menos um quinto do peso.

Para Macedo, esse é o dado mais próximo do efeito de oferecer o tratamento a uma população inteira. Ainda assim, não reproduz exatamente a rotina do consultório, já que um ensaio clínico seleciona os pacientes e os acompanha de perto.

Os efeitos adversos mais comuns foram gastrointestinais, e ficaram mais frequentes à medida que a dose aumentava. Na dose de 12 mg:

Diarreia : atingiu 33,6% dos pacientes, contra 13,2% no grupo placebo.

Náusea : atingiu 28% dos pacientes, contra 8%.

Vômitos : atingiram 15,7% dos pacientes, contra 4,2%.

Segundo Macedo, esses sintomas são característicos dos tratamentos baseados em incretinas, os hormônios intestinais sobre os quais o remédio atua, e aparecem sobretudo nas semanas em que a dose é aumentada. No estudo, todos começaram com 2 mg semanais, e a dose subiu a cada quatro semanas até a meta de cada grupo.

O endocrinologista ressalta que esses números, isoladamente, não permitem dizer se a retatrutida é mais ou menos tolerável que a semaglutida ou a tirzepatida. Para isso, seria preciso comparar os remédios diretamente, nas mesmas condições.

Um efeito menos conhecido também apareceu com mais frequência entre quem usou o remédio. A disestesia é uma alteração da sensibilidade que provoca formigamento, queimação ou desconforto ao toque, sem nenhum estímulo que justifique a sensação. O sintoma ficou mais comum à medida que a dose aumentava:

Entre os pacientes que tomaram a dose de 4 mg, 4,5% tiveram disestesia.

Entre os que tomaram 9 mg, 5,6% tiveram o sintoma.

Entre os que tomaram 12 mg, a dose mais alta, foram 7,3%.

No grupo placebo, apenas 0,7% relataram o problema.

Alterações desse tipo já haviam surgido em estudos anteriores com a retatrutida, mas a causa ainda não é conhecida. De acordo com Macedo, os dados não permitem atribuí-las à ação da molécula sobre o glucagon, nem classificá-las como neuropatia diabética, a lesão nos nervos comum em quem tem diabetes. Ele considera importante acompanhar a intensidade, a duração e a recorrência dos episódios.

As infecções urinárias também foram um pouco mais frequentes na dose mais alta: atingiram 8% dos pacientes, contra 6,6% no placebo.

O artigo registrou ainda episódios de hipotensão, a queda excessiva da pressão arterial. Macedo aponta causas plausíveis que podem atuar ao mesmo tempo: a própria perda de peso, a menor ingestão de comida e de sal, a desidratação provocada por diarreia e vômitos e a necessidade de ajustar remédios para hipertensão. Com os dados disponíveis, um efeito direto da molécula não pode ser descartado.

Parte dos participantes interrompeu o tratamento por causa dos efeitos adversos, e a dose intermediária teve mais desistências que a mais alta:

4 mg: 3,8% dos pacientes interromperam o tratamento.

Segundo o especialista, não há base para concluir que a dose de 9 mg seja menos segura. A diferença pode refletir variação estatística ou características dos participantes de cada grupo, e só uma análise detalhada das causas vai esclarecê-la.

Sete mortes registradas ao longo do estudo foram consideradas sem relação com o medicamento. Macedo explica que essa classificação resulta de uma avaliação clínica de cada caso, mas não prova que o risco seja zero. Um número tão pequeno de eventos também não permite medir o efeito do remédio sobre a mortalidade.

Um estudo com pouco mais de mil pessoas acompanhadas por menos de dois anos deixa perguntas sem resposta. Ainda não se sabe se a disestesia persiste com o uso prolongado, se a pressão baixa aumenta o risco de quedas e se o peso perdido se mantém depois que o tratamento é interrompido.

Eventos raros, que só aparecem em populações maiores, também podem ter escapado, e faltam dados sobre idosos e sobre pacientes que usam muitos medicamentos ao mesmo tempo. Os resultados sobre apneia do sono, avaliados dentro do mesmo estudo, ainda serão divulgados.

A Lilly planeja pedir o registro da retatrutida à Food and Drug Administration (FDA), agência reguladora dos Estados Unidos, no primeiro trimestre de 2027 . Pedidos em outros países, como o Brasil, devem vir depois.

Hoje, a única forma legal de receber a substância é participar de um dos estudos clínicos da fabricante . Mesmo assim, canetas vendidas com esse nome circulam no país. As apreensões de canetas emagrecedoras irregulares feitas pela Receita Federal e pela Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) na região de Foz do Iguaçu, entre elas produtos vendidos como retatrutida, passaram de R$ 11 milhões só no primeiro trimestre de 2026.

Fora dos estudos, não há controle sobre o que o produto contém, e nem os resultados de eficácia nem o perfil de segurança descritos agora na Lancet valem para essas canetas.

articles.title: From 1912 to 1945, a New York landowner planted up to 55,000 trees a year; the experiments helped shape America's tree-planting programmes
articles.summary: Discover how Franklin D. Roosevelt transformed his Hyde Park estate into a thriving tree farm, influencing national reforestation policies through his innovative practices and commitment to forestry.
articles.body: Most people will likely cite sailing or stamp collecting when asked what Franklin D. Roosevelt did to unwind. Foresters typically respond differently. The record demonstrates that Roosevelt took his self-described status as a tree farmer seriously. He spent most of his adult life transforming steep slopes and dilapidated fields into functioning woods on the family property at Hyde Park in the Hudson Valley of New York.People are surprised by the scale. Roosevelt purchased his first saplings in 1912, the year he was appointed chairman of the New York Senate's Forestry Committee, according to the National Park Service. He would plant close to half a million trees over the following three decades. By the 1930s the estate was taking in somewhere between 20,000 and 55,000 new trees a year, and the habit continued until his death in 1945.Behind those numbers sits a bigger question. Was the endeavour a wealthy man's hobby, or something closer to a field experiment that shaped how America thought about reforestation? The evidence leans towards the second.A crop not a viewEventually, the estate swelled to about 1,600 acres. Some 800 acres were native woodlands, 400 acres were orchards, pastures and tilled fields, and the remaining 400 acres were set aside for Roosevelt's tree planting, with about 250 of them carrying established plantations by 1943. The difference was his approach to those plantations. The park agency says he saw his woodlots as a crop rather than scenery, and he wanted the property to stay productive for the long term.He did not labour alone. In 1930 he teamed up with Nelson C. Brown, a professor of forestry at the New York State College of Forestry at Syracuse University. Between 1930 and 1933, the college established 36 plantations with roughly 88,600 trees. After 1933, according to the National Park Service, Brown served for twelve more years as Roosevelt's unofficial and unpaid forest manager, helping him expand the programme and begin Christmas tree production on a large scale.A neighbour had shown what was possible. The conservation group Scenic Hudson cites the railway magnate Archibald Rogers, who planted a tree farm on his Hyde Park estate and gradually trimmed it as the trees matured. Roosevelt learned from the example and then pressed on, with a trained forester at his side.Trees that earned their keepSome plots were purely experimental or demonstration plantings, which turned the estate into what the park service describes as a learning laboratory that gave others data. In 1943 Brown reported the results in the Journal of Forestry, noting that the family woodlands then held 800 acres of natural growth and 250 acres of plantations. The most recent felling had supplied oak and shipbuilding timber for the war effort, a reminder that a gentleman's wood had become a real source of wartime material.Christmas trees were something of a hallmark crop. Roosevelt sent trees from Hyde Park to Winston Churchill, and the NPS archives hold memos to the estate manager, William Plog, about the 1943 Christmas tree gifts. It was a telling detail, and it showed how seriously the operation was run. There were managers, records and a market. He was not simply a man with a shovel.Hyde Park to national policyTo imply that one estate designed America’s tree-planting schemes is going too far. Roosevelt had numerous advisers, and forestry science was rapidly advancing over these decades. But he arrived at the White House fully convinced, from his own soil, that planting trees at scale was practicable, measurable and worth public funds. The best representation of that philosophy is the Civilian Conservation Corps, created in 1933.Let New York's own records tell the tale. The Department of Environmental Conservation says Roosevelt had a specific interest in forestry and began planting his estate with seedlings from the state tree nursery in 1912. The Depression cut state financing for tree planting, but the Corps revived the scheme, planting millions of saplings in barren soil and giving jobs to thousands of young men. Work slowed again during the war years, from 1941 to 1945.The Hyde Park plantings are a handy reminder that big conservation movements often start with someone testing an idea on their own land. Roosevelt planted hundreds of thousands of trees, kept detailed records with professional help, and then carried the same confidence into national policy. Many of those trees still stand in the Hudson Valley today.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Smart glasses have a privacy problem and Meta may have just 'fixed' it
articles.summary: Sometimes, the smartest upgrade is a missing feature.
articles.body: Sometimes, the smartest upgrade is a missing feature. Meta’s decision to launch AI glasses without a camera could do more to broaden their appeal than another improvement in video quality. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition. Announced at Connect 2026 last week, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. Developed with EssilorLuxottica, they offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. These are familiar functions, packaged in something people may already wear every day. The camera’s absence is the selling point.That makes this a sensible move. Technology companies often assume that adding capabilities automatically makes a product more desirable. Wearables complicate that equation because other people have to live with them, too. A device sitting on someone’s face affects the person across the table as much as its owner.Taking the camera out of the conversationMeta’s earlier glasses demonstrated the appeal of recording life without reaching for a phone. For holidays, family moments or content creation, that convenience has obvious value. But the same ease of capture also created an uncomfortable question: how does anyone nearby know whether they are becoming somebody else’s content?Reports of people filming others without consent, including women approached by men wearing the glasses, turned that concern into something tangible. The derogatory “pervert glasses” nickname reflected how quickly a product’s reputation can be shaped by its worst uses. Responsible owners were left carrying some of that reputational burden.Meta introduced safeguards, including updates designed to disable the camera when the recording indicator is tampered with. Those measures matter. But a light requires people to notice it, understand it and trust that it works. It also cannot establish whether someone has agreed to be filmed.Removing the camera offers a much simpler assurance. Buyers do not have to choose between enjoying connected eyewear and carrying a feature they may rarely use but repeatedly have to explain. There is potentially a sizeable audience for that choice: people interested in calls and music who have little desire to document their surroundings.The benefit extends beyond reassuring strangers. Someone might feel more comfortable wearing these glasses around colleagues, at a family gathering or while meeting friends. A useful wearable should slip into everyday routines. If its presence becomes a recurring conversation about surveillance, the convenience starts losing its appeal.There are limits, of course. Camera-free does not mean privacy-free. Microphones and AI services still raise questions about what information is collected, processed and retained. Nor will everyone immediately distinguish the audio model from camera-equipped versions. Meta will need clear communication, but it now has a meaningful hardware difference to explain.A better fit for everyday useThe stronger commercial argument is that audio may be enough. Many prospective buyers could reasonably want to answer a call, hear a podcast or ask a question without taking out their phones. None of those tasks requires a camera. Removing it makes the proposition easier to understand.For people who already wear spectacles, the appeal is particularly straightforward. Adding useful audio functions to an existing habit could feel more natural than finding room for another gadget. Others may welcome an alternative to wearing earbuds. The potential audience includes people who would never describe themselves as early adopters.That brings Meta into a familiar contest with products such as Apple’s Siri-enabled AirPods: which device makes small, repeated tasks easiest? The glasses do not need to replace a smartphone to earn their place. They need to make enough everyday interactions more convenient that wearing them becomes a habit.Muse will face the same practical test. An assistant that responds reliably and saves time could strengthen the product’s appeal. One that requires repeated instructions will quickly become a feature owners ignore. Music and calls provide a useful foundation while buyers decide how much AI they actually want.At $349, Meta still has to justify the purchase. Comfort, sound quality, battery life and reliable calling will matter more than keynote promises. Removing the camera also sacrifices visual AI functions and hands-free photography. Those are worthwhile capabilities, but offering a choice recognises that buyers value them differently.Meta has made a good move because it gives people a reason to reconsider the category. For plenty of buyers, useful glasses that attract less suspicion may be the upgrade they were waiting for.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Anti-South Asian hate speech on X surges 240% in US, Indians at centre amid H-1B row: Report
articles.summary: A new report reveals a staggering 240% increase in online hate speech against South Asians in the U.S., particularly targeting Indians amidst ongoing immigration debates over the H-1B visa program.
articles.body: Hate targeting Indians and other South Asians has risen sharply online in the United States, with a new report linking the increase to immigration politics, economic anxiety and the growing visibility of the community in American public life.The monthly volume of anti-South Asian hate posts on X jumped 240% between January 2024 and June 2026, rising from 12,904 to 43,843, according to a report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH).The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, published on Sunday, examined online posts using the United Nations definition of hate speech. Researchers also reviewed posts to exclude criticism that did not meet that threshold.Researchers found more than 542,000 hateful posts targeting South Asians in the US on X between January 2025 and June 2026. Five of the six months with the highest volume of such posts came towards the end of the period studied.Indians at centre of immigration and jobs debateMore than 70% of H-1B visa holders are Indian, according to the report, making Indians a frequent target when the programme becomes part of the wider immigration debate.Researchers found that nearly half of the hateful posts on X accused South Asians of invading the US, taking jobs or posing a demographic threat.The slur “pajeet” and its variants appeared in 30% of hateful posts on X and 45% of such posts on fringe platforms, the report said.Another recurring theme was portraying South Asians as dirty or unhygienic. Posts pushing that narrative increased 171% on X, the researchers found, making it the fastest-growing narrative tracked in the study.The report also found that Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis were frequently treated as one group online, while different religious communities, including Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Christians, were similarly conflated.H-1B visa row emerges as major flashpointResearchers linked several spikes in anti-South Asian hate to political disputes over the H-1B programme.Last year in September, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions.The report said such actions can reinforce hostility towards South Asians among supporters of Trump’s immigration policies.Researchers also pointed to Trump’s remarks at an AI summit in July 2025, in which he criticized US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India. Anti-South Asian rhetoric sharply increased after his remarks.The study argues that economic concerns have increasingly become intertwined with hostility towards Indian immigrants, particularly around jobs and skilled-worker visas.From ‘model minority’ to target of economic angerThe report also examines how perceptions of Indian Americans have changed online.Indian Americans have long been associated with the “model minority” stereotype, but researchers said some online narratives now portray them as “opportunists and cheats”.South Asians more broadly are also being used as targets for anger over jobs and the economy.Researchers linked this hostility to wider concerns about demographic change and what they described as anxiety among sections of the majority population over a perceived loss of status.The report also connects some of the rhetoric to the “Great Replacement Theory”, a conspiracy theory claiming that white populations in Western countries are being deliberately replaced.South Asian visibility in US politicsThe growing presence of South Asians in American politics has also brought greater visibility.It cites figures including Vice President JD Vance’s wife Usha Vance, politician Vivek Ramaswamy and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.The report said racist attacks have targeted South Asian figures across party lines. It also documented spikes in anti-South Asian and Islamophobic abuse following Mamdani’s primary and mayoral victories.Researchers said the online hostility reflects a broader argument over who belongs in American society.A September 2026 Department of Homeland Security post titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations” featured a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and told him to “get off our roads”.Days later, the Department of Education posted “Make College Football Great Again” after Texas Republican Bo French complained about the presence of South Asians at a University of Texas football game.Researchers said such rhetoric can reinforce the portrayal of South Asians as outsiders who “can never truly belong in the country”.Online hate spills into real-world harassmentThe report also documents cases in which online hostility has moved beyond posts and comments.Researchers found X accounts publishing personal information about South Asians accused of taking jobs or committing visa fraud. Influencers have also confronted people at their homes and workplaces and posted those encounters online.Generative AI has added another layer, with researchers finding content depicting South Asians as “filthy and unclean”, sexually predatory, culturally backward or a demographic threat.The report said online hate does not operate separately from offline hostility.It cited a July incident in Utah in which an Indian Muslim mall employee was repeatedly stabbed in an attack that federal prosecutors charged as a hate crime. In September, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming truck stop.“Online and offline hate can reinforce one another,” researchers wrote, arguing that stereotypes and narratives can move between social media, political discourse, media and everyday life.For Indian Americans, the report identifies immigration, employment, race and demographic change as overlapping areas through which hostility is increasingly expressed online.Its findings suggest that the community’s growing presence in US workplaces, politics and public life has made Indians more visible in some of the country’s most contentious debates, particularly around immigration and the H-1B programme.You use AI every day. articles.title: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear in Sunderland
articles.summary: The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water, police say.
articles.body:
Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.

Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water.

Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said.

The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water.

No other vehicles are believed to have been involved.

Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident".

"Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said.

He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances.

Members of the public have been asked to continue to avoid the area.

Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service, the North East Ambulance Service and RNLI teams were in attendance earlier helping with the rescue efforts.

A spokesperson for Sunderland AFC posted on social media: "At a deeply difficult time for our city, our thoughts are with the families and friends of those who have lost their lives, and everyone affected by this tragedy.

"We also pay tribute to the emergency services and all those who have responded at the scene."

Earlier, North East mayor, Kim McGuinness, said she had asked the incident commander to keep her updated.

Meanwhile Labour MP for Sunderland Central, Lewis Atkinson, said on X: "My thoughts are with everyone involved and their families, and with the emergency services responding to the scene."

articles.title: Meet Ben O'Connor, the 16-year-old who sold 200,000 gift boxes before building an app to help farmers manage their work
articles.summary: Ben O'Connor, aged 16, from a dairy farming family in Co. Down, is already a serial entrepreneur.
articles.body: Ben O'Connor, aged 16, from a dairy farming family in Co. Down, is already a serial entrepreneur. He set up his first business, a firewood venture, at 11, and at 13 founded Giftery, a mail-order gift basket business that went on to sell 200,000 gift boxes within three years. His latest project, FarmFlow, is farm management software he plans to make available for free, with a free tier always on offer. In an interview with Agriland, Ben O'Connor said: "This year I set up FarmFlow." The product is in a "long soft launch" and will relaunch in August with offline use.How did Ben O'Connor sell 200,000 gift boxes at 16Agriland reports that O'Connor's first "major" business was Giftery, a mail-order gift basket venture. It was set up when he was 13, and it went on to sell 200,000 units within three years.Running the business came with challenges. "It can be hard to get respect when you're a lot younger than the people you're going into meetings with," O'Connor said. Agriland adds that the Giftery experience did teach him to "not give up".On his latest project, O'Connor said: "This year I set up FarmFlow." According to Agriland, the product aims to manage tasks for farmers or, in his words, "to try to solve problems with a farm". He named issues as wide-ranging as relief milkers, feed rations and livestock weight tracking, saying "there's no real thing that brings them together".He said FarmFlow "learns over time" and is "intended to adapt towards the farm". The product is in its early stages but is usable at present, and farmers are invited to take part in a "long soft launch". O'Connor said: "The system can hold only so many, so we're sort of trying to keep numbers limited while we further test it." He added that, once it is fully launched, "anyone who wants it, we would be more than happy to have them".How will FarmFlow work offline on farmers' phonesOne planned feature is offline use. O'Connor said the app is currently web-based for demos but will relaunch in August, working offline with data stored locally within the phone. He said operational data is encrypted and "never leaves end-to-end encryption", adding: "We're figuring out how to make it better."O'Connor plans for FarmFlow to be "completely free", though there will be "revenue models in it". He said: "There'll always be a free tier available because I understand the problems that many farms have with cash flow." Agriland reports that paid-for features are planned for the full launch. O'Connor also has his GCSEs ahead of him and an apprenticeship starting in September, but says FarmFlow remains "a priority". "I'm just trying to balance those things at the moment," he said, adding: "I'll always be entrepreneurial."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2002, a 3.5km sea wall was breached in five places at a 283-hectare Essex arable farm; seawater returned to the land, creating new habitat and helping double saltmarsh across the Greater Thames estuary
articles.summary: A 3.5km stretch of sea wall along the Essex coast was deliberately breached in five places in October 2002.
articles.body: A 3.5km stretch of sea wall along the Essex coast was deliberately breached in five places in October 2002. This allowed tides to rush into 283 hectares of farmland at Abbotts Hall Farm in Great Wigborough. The planned flooding changed an intensively farmed arable site into a thriving coastal wetland. In the years that followed, it doubled the area of saltmarsh across the Greater Thames estuary. The major project, led by Essex Wildlife Trust with strong support from the Heritage Lottery Fund and the World Wide Fund for Nature, became a leading example of coastal realignment in the United Kingdom. Decades after the first breach, the site still shows how controlled seawater can create important wildlife habitats while providing a cost-effective way to defend the coast against rising sea levels.Restoring saltmarsh to defend coastal landSaltmarshes are important natural defences against coastal erosion. They absorb wave energy before tidal surges can reach towns and farmland inland. In the past, large areas of saltmarsh in East Anglia were enclosed and drained so concrete sea walls could be built and more land could be used for farming. According to reports published by the Institution of Civil Engineers, almost a quarter of all saltmarshes in Essex were lost to erosion and man-made structures during the late 20th century. By allowing seawater to cover arable fields below the high-tide level, conservationists wanted to reverse this loss. Engineers cut five separate gaps in the earth wall protecting Abbotts Hall Farm. The incoming sea covered about 80 hectares of low-lying farmland during the first spring tides. This created a network of tidal creeks, mudflats and saltmarsh plants. Because the land naturally rises behind the old wall, intertidal habitats were able to return on their own without major earthmoving work behind the former sea wall.Financial backing and site acquisitionThe purchase of Abbotts Hall Farm, a 730-acre property on the northern bank of the Salcott estuary near Colchester, was made possible by major outside funding. The National Lottery Heritage Fund provided a large grant to secure the site for long-term conservation. Extra funding from the World Wide Fund for Nature, the Environment Agency and English Nature helped pay for the land purchase, early environmental studies and continuing scientific monitoring. Documents from the National Lottery Heritage Fund say that buying the site allowed researchers to carry out one of the largest coastal restoration experiments ever attempted in Europe. Instead of spending millions of pounds repeatedly raising old concrete defences, the team put resources into long-term and more sustainable habitat management. The land purchase also created the permanent headquarters of Essex Wildlife Trust. It provided an education centre alongside the new nature reserve.Rapid ecological recovery along the estuaryEcological monitoring after the 2002 breach found rapid increases in biodiversity across the flooded farmland. Marine invertebrates moved into the newly deposited silt within months. They created a rich food source for migrating waterfowl and resident wading birds. Surveys by the Environment Agency and marine research institutes found that young fish, including bass, herring and sprat, entered the flooded creeks at high tide. The shallow saltwater pools became important nursery areas. They gave young fish shelter from larger predators in the open estuary. Plant surveys recorded the natural spread of saltmarsh plants, including glasswort, sea lavender and saltmarsh grass. As these plants became established, they helped hold the soft mud in place. They also trapped sediment carried in by seawater, slowly raising the ground level over time. Research compiled by the European Centre for River Restoration found that the project doubled saltmarsh coverage across the wider Greater Thames region. The results showed that managed realignment could help stop coastal habitat loss without causing erosion on nearby properties.Combining sustainable agriculture with nature conservationA key aim of the project was to show that managed realignment could work alongside commercial farming instead of ending rural livelihoods. Essex Wildlife Trust kept farming on the higher, unflooded land around the marshes. Shepherds brought sheep onto the upper saltmarsh and coastal grasslands, producing premium saltmarsh lamb. The trust also tested specialist crops that could grow in salty soils, including wild samphire collected from the upper intertidal areas. The project helped influence policy across the Environment Agency and Defra. It encouraged coastal managers across Britain to use nature-based solutions rather than depend only on concrete sea walls. By giving tidal water more room to spread safely, the managed breach reduced pressure on nearby sea walls during storms. This helped protect nearby communities and farmland from uncontrolled flooding. The site remains a working example of how vulnerable, low-lying coastlines can adapt to climate change.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Utah man who spent 41 years behind bars after being sentenced to death in a 1985 murder case has been ordered released on bail after new DNA tests excluded him from crime-scene evidence
articles.summary: A 71-year-old man who spent 41 years on death row has been ordered released on bail by a Utah judge after new DNA testing excluded him from evidence found
articles.body: A 71-year-old man who spent 41 years on death row has been ordered released on bail by a Utah judge after new DNA testing excluded him from evidence found at the crime scene. Douglas Stewart Carter was released from the Utah County Jail in Spanish Fork on Monday evening after a bond hearing in the 4th District Court in Provo. State prosecutors said forensic reports received on 22 September showed no match between Carter and genetic material found on the handle of a knife used in the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen, or blood found on a doorknob at the scene. According to court filings reported by Associated Press, Utah County prosecutors withdrew their notice to seek the death penalty last week. Utah County prosecutor Erwin Petilos told the court that reviewing Carter’s bail conditions was "necessary and fair" while authorities examine the remaining evidence.Landmark ruling following decades of appealsJudge Derek Pullan ordered Carter’s release under strict conditions. These include mandatory electronic GPS monitoring and a ban on any contact with the victim’s family. Judge Pullan said in his ruling that the latest scientific results further weakened the state’s original case. However, he added that a jury could still consider the remaining circumstantial evidence and find Carter guilty. Defence attorney Neal Hamilton confirmed that Carter, a Chicago native who has maintained his innocence throughout four decades of imprisonment, would stay at an extended-stay residence near his son, Tyler Anger.Speaking after the ruling, Hamilton described the serious toll of the case, as reported by News4Jax: "If the state of Utah had their way, he would have been executed 15, 20 years ago before we discovered the misconduct. It's not just as simple as, 'Let's let him go.' He's being released with 41 years of state-induced trauma and the effect it will have on him is very real."His son, who was adopted as an infant and only learned his father’s identity years later, waited outside the facility before the release. Anger told reporters outside the jail that his main focus was helping his father adjust to freedom. He noted that Carter had not set foot on grass in 40 years.Misconduct and recanted witness testimonyThe victim, Eva Olesen, was the aunt of the Provo police chief at the time of her death on 27 February 1985. She was found dead in her home after being bound, stabbed and shot. No physical evidence linked Carter to the crime scene during his original trial in 1985. A jury convicted Carter, who is Black, based on a signed confession and testimony from two key witnesses who said he had boasted about the murder. Carter later said police officers forced him to sign the statement during an interrogation in Nashville, Tennessee, where he was arrested four months after the killing. The case began to fall apart in 2011 when defence investigators found the two key witnesses in Mexico. Both later admitted under oath that they had lied during the trial after receiving cash payments and help with utility fees from local police officers. They also said investigators had threatened them and their child with deportation if they did not accuse Carter. The witnesses later recanted their testimony. The Utah Supreme Court formally overturned Carter’s conviction last year. The court cited widespread intentional misconduct by police investigators and a prosecutor and ordered a full retrial.Victim's family expresses concernsThe decision to grant bail faced opposition from members of the victim’s family, who raised strong objections during the court proceedings. Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of the victim, spoke to the court and questioned what the forensic testing meant. As reported by Associated Press, she urged the court to keep Carter detained before any future trial: "By golly we were hoping for a concrete match. It doesn't mean he wasn't there. There are other factors and hopefully the investigation will continue. We just want justice for Eva. And if he had any part of it we want that to be known."Defence lawyers had previously filed court documents describing other suspects from the original 1985 investigation. These included claims that eyewitnesses saw a white man fleeing the scene. They argued that investigators hid evidence that pointed away from Carter during the early stages of the murder investigation. Current reporting also identifies the victim’s husband, Orla Olesen, as a potential alternative suspect raised by the defence. A two-month retrial remains provisionally scheduled for 2027. However, defence lawyers said they plan to file formal requests asking for all pending aggravated murder charges to be dismissed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump’s own America.gov chatbot contradicts US president on 2020 polls, climate
articles.summary: The AI-powered America.gov website launched by US President Donald Trump on Tuesday gave factual answers to several politically sensitive questions,
articles.body: The AI-powered America.gov website launched by US President Donald Trump on Tuesday gave factual answers to several politically sensitive questions, including some that contradicted claims made by the president.According to Associated Press, the website, launched to make government information and services easier to access, initially answered questions about the 2020 election, Trump’s possible 2028 presidential bid, climate change and presidential salaries.On the 2020 election, the chatbot said: “Official federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. Isolated election crimes did occur and have been prosecuted.”Trump has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that the 2020 election was “stolen” from him. Audits and recounts did not find widespread fraud that changed the result.Asked whether Trump could run for president again in 2028, the chatbot cited the 22nd Amendment, saying: “The 22nd Amendment says that no person shall be elected President more than twice. Donald J Trump has already been elected twice (2016 and 2024). I am not giving legal advice.”Trump has repeatedly floated the possibility of seeking a third term despite the constitutional limit.The chatbot also identified the Pentagon as “the headquarters of the department of defense”, despite Trump’s push to use the name Department of War.On climate change, the site said: “Federal climate-science pages say recent warming is largely from human greenhouse-gas emissions, mainly burning fossil fuels. Earth’s climate has also changed for natural reasons over long periods.”Trump has previously called climate change a “hoax”.The chatbot also challenged Trump’s claim that he was the first president to forgo his salary. It said that “some presidents have declined to keep that pay,” and listed George Washington, Herbert Hoover and John F Kennedy as presidents who had refused their salaries before Trump.Trump made the claim again during remarks on Tuesday, saying he was the first US president to give up his salary.You use AI every day. articles.title: INDIA bloc meet: 'United' opposition to step up attack on EC, BJP - what's on agenda
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc is set to meet for the second time in four months on Wednesday to chalk out its response to the alleged differences within the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc is set to meet for the second time in four months on Wednesday to chalk out its response to the alleged differences within the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.The opposition parties are likely to finalise a joint action plan, including an agitation against the EC's voter-roll exercise and a demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.What's on agendaThe opposition will prepare a draft notice for a fresh bid to move a motion in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha for the removal of the CEC and deliberate on its approval at the meeting, sources told news agency PTI.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan had rejected the opposition's first notice, which was signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members, seeking the CEC's removal over alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Meanwhile, a notice moved by 73 opposition MPs from Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal is already pending in the Upper House of Parliament.Article 324(5) of the Constitution states that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only "in like manner and on like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court."Who is attendingCongress president Mallikarjun Kharge, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress parliamentary party chairperson Sonia Gandhi are expected to attend the opposition meeting.West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and Abhishek Banerjee are also expected to join. RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah and PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti are among the other leaders likely to participate.The Left parties are also expected to be represented, with CPM Rajya Sabha floor leader John Brittas likely to attend. Leaders of the CPI, CPI(ML), RSP and other Left parties are expected to join as well.Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray is likely to participate virtually due to prior engagements in Mumbai, including a campaign against the Election Commission.NCP (SP) leader Supriya Sule and leaders of smaller opposition parties, including the JMM, IUML, VCK, MDMK, Kerala Congress factions, RLP, BAP, Lok Dal and Forward Bloc, are also expected to attend.Independent Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal is likely to participate in the deliberations.Who is skippingSamajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav is unlikely to attend in person. The party is expected to send senior leaders instead. Reports said Akhilesh cited commitments linked to the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh and other prior engagements.The absence comes amid differences between the SP and Congress over seat-sharing discussions for the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.The Aam Aadmi Party, DMK and Biju Janata Dal are among the parties that will not attend the meeting.The AAP was part of the INDIA bloc's 2024 Lok Sabha alliance but has since distanced itself from the grouping.The DMK, a Congress ally in Tamil Nadu, has also decided to stay away. DMK spokesperson TKS Elangovan said the party remained aligned with the opposition on several issues but was no longer part of the INDIA bloc.
