articles.title: Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises
articles.summary: Ethiopia accuses Sudan and Egypt of backing armed groups, deepening tensions amid internal unrest.
articles.body:
As renewed fighting spreads across northern Ethiopia, the government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing armed opposition groups, raising fears that the conflict could draw in regional powers.

Over the weekend, Ethiopian army chief Birhanu Jula attributed his country’s unrest to those he called Ethiopia’s “historical and contemporary adversaries”.

Birhanu accused Eritrea of being the go-between linking these external powers – including Sudan and Egypt, which he explicitly named – with armed groups inside Ethiopia.

Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt have all rejected the accusations. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Egyptian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Nader Zaki said that Egypt’s foreign policy was founded on “full respect for the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states, and noninterference in the internal affairs of other countries”.

Zaki added that Egypt “is fully committed to the rules of international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and rejects any practices that would undermine regional security and stability”.

Major-General Samir Farag, the former head of the Egyptian Armed Forces’ Morale Affairs Department, also told Al Jazeera that the accusations against Egypt were false. “It has not been Egypt’s policy to interfere in the internal affairs of any state in the region,” he said.

Sudan’s military also dismissed the accusations as “baseless” and levelled its own charge of destabilising behaviour at Ethiopia, accusing it of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces since 2023. Ethiopia has denied those allegations.

Ethiopia’s relations with the countries it has accused have already been strained by other disputes that predate the latest fighting.

Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa have remained tense as a longstanding dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) remains unresolved. Competition between the two has increasingly extended to regional security, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa.

Sudan’s relations with Ethiopia are similarly troubled. Since the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war, Khartoum has accused Addis Ababa of providing training, supplies and the use of Ethiopian territory to the RSF.

Eritrea had fought alongside Ethiopia against rebel groups in the latter’s Tigray region during a war between 2020 and 2022, but relations between the two neighbours have since soured, with Eritrea alarmed by Ethiopia’s attempts to gain access to the Red Sea.

Against that background, some analysts and Ethiopian opposition figures say that Addis Ababa is pointing the finger at foreign conspiracies in a bid to rally support behind its national army.

Mohamed Selim, deputy chair of the Egyptian parliament’s African Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that he believes the accusations were an attempt to shift attention from Ethiopia’s domestic problems by creating an external enemy and seeking to unify the internal front.

Amani al-Tawil, director of the Africa Programme at the Al-Ahram Centre for Political and Strategic Studies, similarly described the accusations as “an understandable attempt to escape from internal crises”.

She questioned why Egypt would choose this moment to intervene militarily in Ethiopia, given the two have been in dispute over GERD since 2011.

Al-Tawil said the breadth of the new opposition alliance in Ethiopia – seven groups representing disparate ethnic groups and regions announced the coalition last week – presented a challenge to Addis Ababa.

The renewed fighting in Ethiopia has spread across Tigray and into neighbouring Amhara and Afar.

Mohammed Hussein, the chairman of the Prosperity Party Afar Region Branch Office – the ruling party in Ethiopia’s Afar region – told Al Jazeera that the three regions together have a population of more than 38 million, according to his estimate, and include areas near the borders with Djibouti and Eritrea, raising fears of a regional war.

Ammar Arki, a writer focusing on Horn of Africa affairs, told Al Jazeera that Ethiopia had, at various stages, blamed Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea for contributing to instability inside Ethiopia.

He said the latest accusations could be interpreted as an attempt to redirect some domestic attention towards an external threat and build support around the federal government.

But Arki warned that the longer Addis Ababa continued to explain its internal crisis in terms of an “external conspiracy”, particularly if neighbouring states responded in the same way, the greater the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict could move beyond Ethiopia’s borders and become regional.

articles.title: Prince William and Catherine's surprise visit to Kevin Sinfield's charity run
articles.summary: The rugby league star is on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease charities.
articles.body:
The Prince and Princess of Wales made a surprise visit to support rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield, on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities.

"What you're doing is so inspiring – the unity that you're building," Catherine told Sir Kevin.

Prince William and Catherine caught up with Sir Kevin in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, as he carries out what he says will be his final fundraising challenge.

Sir Kevin is aiming to complete seven ultra marathons in seven days, running between Hull and Manchester, in a challenge inspired by his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from MND in 2024.

The rugby star's gruelling mission will end on Saturday at Old Trafford in Manchester, when Sir Kevin arrives ahead of the Super League Grand Final.

"Make sure you hold yourself together for another few days," Prince William told him.

Sir Kevin replied that he had been dreaming of an ice bath all day.

Since his first challenge in 2020, Sir Kevin has raised more than £11m for MND causes - and Prince William and Catherine made a private donation to the charity effort.

Before meeting Sir Kevin, the royal couple talked to families facing the impact of MND and heard how fundraising projects had helped them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Prince William and Catherine visited the home ground of Rob Burrow's rugby league team, Leeds Rhinos, and met some young players.

The royal visitors heard how the club's charitable foundation was working to help health, education and well-being projects in the Leeds area.

Jamie Jones-Buchanan, a former teammate of Rob Burrow, described the team's ethos in good and bad times: "We went through success and adversity, but we always came out on the other side together."

Prince William and Catherine have previously supported Sir Kevin's efforts for MND charities - and the prince had presented Sir Kevin and Rob Burrow with their CBEs at the Leeds Rhinos ground in Headingley in January 2024.

Rob Burrow died in June that year, aged 41, with Prince William among those paying tribute .

This was the second royal endorsement this week for Sir Kevin's charity run - with Princess Anne having shown her support for him on Monday at the University of York.

Although Princess Anne observed that the term "fun run" was a contradiction in terms.

"I can run but I don't do it for fun. I'm past that stage," she told Sir Kevin.

The knighthood awarded to Sir Kevin this year was among the first for a rugby league player.

There had been accusations that the honours system had been ignoring rugby league out of snobbishness.

But in June 2025, Sir Billy Boston became a rugby league knight - the first in the sport's 130-year history.

articles.title: In 1964, an Arizona couple began building a carport with discarded bottles; years later, the project had grown into a 2,700-sq-ft home made with thousands of bottles and listed for $432,500
articles.summary: A Tucson couple’s simple plan to build a shelter for a family car in 1964 grew into a 2,700-square-foot home made from tens of thousands of discarded
articles.body: A Tucson couple’s simple plan to build a shelter for a family car in 1964 grew into a 2,700-square-foot home made from tens of thousands of discarded glass bottles. The unusual property has now been put on the market for $432,500 (£342,000). Located in Tucson, Arizona, the hand-built house has thick mortar walls filled with green wine bottles, amber beer bottles and cobalt blue medicine jars collected from local roadsides, bars and landfills. According to the Arizona Daily Star, local residents Howard and Joy Finch built the property over several decades, turning discarded materials into a lasting desert landmark. The property was later owned by artist Kathe B, who maintained the home after the original builders. Architectural Digest reported that sunlight passing through the coloured bottle bases set into the walls creates a natural stained-glass effect inside the house.Building a home out of roadside wasteIn 1964, Howard Finch decided to build a simple covered carport behind his existing home. He used leftover glass bottles set in concrete. After finding that the method was both strong and attractive, the couple expanded their plans and began building a complete custom home on the desert property. For almost two decades, the couple collected unwanted glass across the Tucson basin. According to the Arizona Daily Star, the Finches placed every bottle by hand. They laid the bottles horizontally in thick layers of mortar to create strong outside and inside walls. Friends, family members and local business owners also helped by bringing empty bottles and containers to the site. The couple cleaned each piece of glass before putting it into the mortar. This helped keep the growing walls strong and stable. The finished main house has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and an open-plan artist studio. Architectural Digest noted that green wine bottles, brown beer bottles and blue Milk of Magnesia containers form different decorative patterns throughout the living rooms, kitchen and surrounding courtyards.Natural cooling in the Sonoran DesertThe unusual building method was not only about appearance. It also served a practical purpose in southern Arizona’s extreme climate. The Sonoran Desert has very hot summers and sharp temperature drops at night. As reported by the Arizona Daily Star, the thick mix of glass and concrete gives the home significant thermal mass. The heavy walls absorb heat during the day, helping keep the rooms cool. They then slowly release that heat back into the house during cold desert nights. The empty space inside each sealed bottle also provides natural insulation. This helped reduce energy use long before modern green building methods became common in homes. The house also contains other recycled materials collected during the mid-20th century. These include salvaged timber beams, decorative ironwork and stone paving blocks taken from regional demolition sites.Preserving a piece of regional folk architectureAfter the Finches’ time at the property, artist Kathe B bought the home and carefully restored it. She worked to protect the original glasswork while updating the plumbing and electrical systems to meet modern building standards. The property listing, handled by local firm Long Realty, offered the 2,700-square-foot home on a multi-acre desert lot. The land has mature saguaro cacti, mesquite trees and views of the Catalina Mountains. The sale also included the main bottle house and a separate workshop built with similar recycled materials. Architectural Digest reported that the property attracted interest from folk art enthusiasts and buyers looking for unusual homes. Several folk-art buildings made from recycled materials exist across North America, but few remain structurally sound or approved for full-time residential use six decades after construction began. The Tucson property remains a fully working example of mid-century American folk architecture. It shows how two local residents turned everyday waste into a permanent home.Folk art traditions across the American WestThe Finch house is part of a wider tradition of unusual desert architecture that developed across the American West during the mid-20th century. During this period, creative builders often experimented with cheap materials such as glass bottles, tin cans and rammed earth to make off-grid shelters. Architectural historians interviewed by the Arizona Daily Star said glass bottle construction dates back to early mining towns in Nevada and California. Timber was scarce in these areas, but empty bottles from saloons were easy to find. Builders in the early 1900s discovered that bottles stacked in mud or mortar could create cheap walls that let light through and could withstand strong desert winds. The Finch house is one of the largest and most complete residential examples of this building style in Arizona. Local preservation groups, including the Tucson Historic Preservation Foundation, have described the property as an irreplaceable cultural resource. They say it captures the independent spirit of post-war Tucson.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Andy Burnham pledges pension triple lock changes to fund care reforms
articles.summary: The PM was at times emotional during his conference speech in which he outlined his long-term plan for the UK.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has set out his plan to transform Britain, including by ending the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 to help fund a new national care service.

In his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister, Burnham also said he wants to pave the way for greater public control over housing, water and energy services, and potentially reform the UK's electoral system.

After days of questions over how to fund his social care reforms in England, Burnham pointed to changing the triple lock to generate "significant savings".

His plans would see the state pension increase every year at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

Andy Burnham: Northern PM's long journey to power

In front of a packed hall and watched on by family and friends, Burnham spoke for more than an hour - at times pausing and appearing to hold back tears as he referred to his father, Roy, who died earlier this month .

Arriving on stage to the sound of "All Together Now" by Liverpool band The Farm, Burnham made the song title a theme of his speech.

He said he wanted to "draw a line on a decade of division" and to "stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down".

Burnham also told conference that he wants to "put the country on a new path" and recalled his family's "working-class aspiration" and how the government wanted to "unlock" this for others.

There was an expectation that Burnham's time in Liverpool for his party's conference would see him flesh out his vision for the future of the country.

In the conference hall, he offered more details albeit with some of the proposals relating to the content of the Labour manifesto at the next general election rather than delivering immediate action.

Burnham's plan to offer free at the point of use social care in England is among those being developed so it can be put before voters in 2029. He said it would be "fully funded and not through borrowing".

Explaining his long-held ambition to make changes, he raised his family's experiences - including how his grandmother Kitty's engagement ring was "ripped from her finger and stolen in a care home".

He argued a national care service was a "landmark" policy that would be "as significant as the creation of the NHS itself and utterly essential to securing its future".

Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off".

The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest.

Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it".

He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation.

"But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service.

"Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care changes today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen."

Officials have suggested the change could save £15bn a year by 2040.

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time".

He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners".

Elsewhere in his speech, Burnham said he wanted to repeal "Margaret Thatcher's ideological ban on public ownership of water companies".

The PM said legislation will be put before Parliament, adding the changes will "start a 10-year journey to a very different water system", which includes new powers for mayors to hold "companies to account".

Burnham said it will be made easier for councils to acquire private rented homes in poor condition if landlords refuse to take action after being issued warnings.

He said the government will change the law "if necessary".

Burnham also told delegates that "Brexit has done more harm than good" before he indicated he wanted to explore closer UK-EU ties.

Ahead of talks expected later this year with EU chiefs, Burnham said he would set out the "different options" for Britain's "long-term relationship" with the bloc.

He said: "I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in."

To cheers in the hall, Burnham announced a national commission on electoral reform , which could result in changes to the current voting system for UK parliamentary elections.

He asked all political parties to contribute to the work of the commission, adding: "We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard."

In response, Skills Minister Baroness Smith of Malvern told the PA news agency: "Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities. Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested in what it comes out with."

Burnham also said he wants to "invest" in young people and change the education system and welfare system.

He said: "We will rebuild a system of comprehensive education in this country, with parity between academic and technical."

Burnham added there needs to be a "fundamental rethink" of the welfare system to fund new opportunities for young people.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the PM's conference speech contained little more than "half measures, reannouncements and tinkering".

articles.body: United States on Tuesday offered to loan energy companies 40 million barrels of oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an attempt to control rising prices due to the Ukraine and Iran conflict.In March, the United States committed to lend 172 million barrels of oil from the SPR, forming part of a broader agreement among roughly 30 International Energy Agency member countries to release 400 million barrels in total.In June, the Trump administration offered to lend the final 40 million barrels under that IEA arrangement. Later that month, however, it disclosed that companies had agreed to borrow only around 500,000 barrels.The move comes amid an energy crisis that has erupted due to the escalating Russia-Ukraine war, and America’s inconclusive conflict with Iran.Ukraine has been increasingly targeting Russian energy facilities in order to curb the financial resources that sustain Russian war efforts.On Sunday night, it struck oil facilities in Russia’s Krasnodar region."We are consistently using our long-range capabilities to respond to Russian strikes", Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, adding that Moscow must stop escalating the conflict.Oil strain on IndiaMeanwhile, Reuters reported on Tuesday that Indian refiners expect Russian oil supplies to decline further in October and November.Lower Russian exports and fierce competition from China are forcing the country to buy costlier alternatives for the rest of the year."Demand from China has been really high. They were willing to book cargoes in advance and to pay firmer prices compared to Indian refiners," said a source involved in the sale of Russian crude.Analytics firm Kpler expects Russian oil arrivals in India to fall to about 1.75 million barrels per day in September, the lowest level since April. Trade data showed that arrivals had already dropped 16.5 per cent from July to around 2.1 million bpd in August, though Russia remained India's main supplier, ahead of the UAE and Venezuela.The overall availability of Russian exports has reportedly shrunk, especially from the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, where shipments have roughly halved because repeated drone attacks have suspended loadings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Schoolboy kills teacher, injures two in Slovakia school stabbing
articles.summary: Police detain the 13-year-old in the northwestern village of Staskov, launch investigation into ‘premeditated murder’.
articles.body:
A 13-year-old elementary schoolboy has stabbed a 61-year-old female teacher dead in northwestern Slovakia, according to authorities.

A 44-year-old female teacher and a schoolgirl were also seriously wounded in Tuesday’s attack in the village of Staskov, near the Czech border, emergency service spokeswoman Petra Klimesova told the AFP news agency.

Health Minister Kamil Sasko told reporters the schoolgirl was “in a serious, critical condition”.

Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok said at a news conference in Staskov that the life of the second teacher who was stabbed in the chest was not in danger.

A motive for the attack was not immediately known.

Police said the attacker was arrested and is being investigated by the Office for Combating Organised Crime (UBOK) for “premeditated murder”.

The situation in the village with a population of about 2,750 people was “under control”, according to the law enforcement service.

Sutaj Estok praised the head teacher who was present at the scene and said, “she followed every single procedure outlined in the available manuals to the letter and prevented the tragedy from becoming even worse.”

Prime Minister Robert Fico expressed his “sincere condolences” and said he was following “the tragic incident in the village of Staskov with great concern”.

“Personally, I am deeply saddened by this,” he said in a statement.

President Peter Pellegrini said he was “shocked that this is yet another case in which a student attacked teachers and a classmate”.

“Aggression and an atmosphere of intolerance – spread primarily by social media and, unfortunately, by some politicians as well – are literally poisoning the public sphere and influencing the behaviour of our children in schools,” he said.

He urged “all citizens to act in a way that calms the atmosphere, rather than further radicalising it”.

Last year, an 18-year-old student fatally stabbed a 51-year-old deputy principal and an 18-year-old student at a high school in northern Slovakia.

In 2020, a 22-year-old former student attacked a high school in the town of Vrutky, killing the deputy principal and wounding five people, including two students.

In 2022, a high school student attacked and injured a female pupil at a high school in Novaky.

articles.title: Morocco’s king names Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri first woman PM
articles.summary: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri becomes the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world.
articles.body:
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has named Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country’s first female prime minister and the second-woman ever in the Arab world to serve in the position.

The royal palace said in a statement on Tuesday that El Mansouri, a 50-year-old urban planning minister and the mayor of Marrakesh, was tasked with forming a new government.

El Mansouri said in a televised address her appointment was “truly historic”.

“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government,” she said. “This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women.”

The appointment came four days after the results of last week’s elections were announced, with El Mansouri’s monarchy-aligned Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) winning the most votes to secure 97 of the 395 seats in the House of Representatives, Morocco’s lower house of parliament.

PAM fell well short of the 198 seats needed for an outright majority and will need to build a coalition in order to govern, which will be El Mansouri’s first task.

PAM, founded in 2008 by Fouad Ali El Himma, a friend of the king, has expressed its willingness to work with all parties. But some, including the Justice and Development Party (PJD) and Federation of Democratic Left, have announced they will remain in the opposition.

This governing coalition will decide allocations for billions of dollars in investments ahead of the 2030 FIFA World Cup, scheduled to be primarily hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain.

El Mansouri is the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden’s tenure in Tunisia from October 2021 to August 2023.

Born in Marrakesh in 1976, El Mansouri studied law, obtaining a diploma in advanced studies from the University of Montpellier in France, as well as a diploma in Anglo-Saxon business law from New York University in the United States.

She entered local governance early, when she was elected mayor of Marrakesh in 2009, becoming the first woman to hold the city’s mayoralty.

After the end of her first term, she returned to lead the Marrakesh municipal council following the 2021 elections. She also accumulated parliamentary experience, being elected as a member of the House of Representatives over successive terms.

In October 2021, El Mansouri moved into national government, appointed as Minister of National Spatial Planning, Urban Development, Housing and Urban Policy.

During her tenure, this portfolio was associated with a number of key files, including the direct housing support programme, reforms linked to urban planning and spatial development and the file on rehousing those affected by the Al Haouz earthquake.

articles.title: Chris Hansen rips Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ as ‘complete fiction,’ reveals how he’s fighting back
articles.summary: Chris Hansen accuses A24's "Primetime" of fictionalizing his "To Catch a Predator" investigations and says he bought ads running on 3,500 screens.
articles.body: Chris Hansen is pushing back against Hollywood's portrayal of his career in the new A24 film, "Primetime," saying the movie fictionalizes the work that made "To Catch a Predator" a television phenomenon. "Nothing in that trailer except for the actor saying my name and ‘have a seat’ ever happened in real life. It’s complete fiction," Hansen said during an interview on the "Planet Tyrus" podcast. The A24 feature, released Friday, offers a dramatization inspired by Hansen's hit "To Catch a Predator" investigations, including events surrounding the death of Bill Conradt, a Texas chief felony assistant district attorney who died by suicide as police arrived at his home to execute search and arrest warrants stemming from an online sting. The film stars Robert Pattinson as Hansen, portraying the television host as he pursues greater exposure for the program while its increasingly high-stakes investigations propel him toward greater fame and, ultimately, the Conradt incident. 'PRIMETIME' STAR ROBERT PATTINSON SHOCKS FANS WITH CHRIS HANSEN TRANSFORMATION IN 'UNSETTLING' TRAILER Hansen said the film distorts the work he and others have done to expose adults seeking to sexually exploit children, arguing that Hollywood is using his name and the popularity of the franchise to sell a fictionalized version of events. "It’s shocking and a bit of an insult, based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer, based upon what other people have told me about the film… It’s an insult to turn something that’s been so positive and so important into a dark, over-dramatized [portrayal]…" he told Tyrus. "It's Hollywood twisting what happened..." he added. Hansen said he had not seen the film at the time of the interview and had no input in its production. He said he had no issue with Pattinson, adding that he considers him a "good actor" who has been "very gracious" to him. Instead, Hansen directed his criticism at the filmmakers and Hollywood more broadly, invoking former film producer and convicted sex offender Harvey Weinstein. "What do you expect out of an industry that was led for years by one of the most prolific predators to walk the face of the earth, Harvey Weinstein?" he asked. To combat what he views as an inaccurate portrayal, Hansen said he purchased ad slots before showings of "Primetime," in which he will "walk into [a] kitchen, tell everybody in the theater to have a seat" and remind them that the "real work continues every day" on his true-crime streaming service, TruBlu. CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS Hansen said the 30-second ads will run on 3,500 screens nationwide during the film's first month, which he said will allow him to use the movie's release to direct audiences toward the work he says Hollywood misrepresented. Meanwhile, Hansen is also preparing to tell his side of the story through a documentary titled "I’m Chris Hansen," which he said recently finished production and is being shopped to streaming platforms. Unlike "Primetime," Hansen said he cooperated with that project and knew the filmmakers involved. Director Lance Oppenheim has defended his decision not to involve Hansen in the production of "Primetime." When asked by W Magazine why he did not consult Hansen while making the film, Oppenheim said he believed Hansen's existing work and public record provided what he needed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I felt like I had everything I needed with the Cameo," Oppenheim said, referring to a $30 personalized video Hansen recorded for him in 2024 after the director's wife purchased it as a gift. Oppenheim said he also read Hansen's book and blog and spoke with Mitchell Wagenberg, a hidden-camera operator who worked with Hansen on "To Catch a Predator." "It almost felt like we were adapting the Internet's version of Chris Hansen rather than the real Chris Hansen," Oppenheim said. "You can self-mythologize all you want, but at a certain point it becomes part of culture." "The Odyssey wasn’t told by Odysseus. This movie shouldn’t be told by Chris Hansen. It should be told by the fans of Chris Hansen, which is us," he added.

articles.title: Meet Austin Koziarski, the high-school student who now leads more than 200 volunteers helping refugee children across 18 schools
articles.summary: When Austin Koziarski first arrived at JaxTHRIVE as a high school freshman, he was looking for a way to spend his time on something useful.
articles.body: When Austin Koziarski first arrived at JaxTHRIVE as a high school freshman, he was looking for a way to spend his time on something useful. The Jacksonville programme allowed him to tutor children who had recently arrived in the United States, including many from Afghanistan. What began as a volunteering role gradually became a much larger commitment. articles.title: Sunny Hostin addresses resurfaced reports questioning her claim she was a holdout juror in 1991 murder trial
articles.summary: Sunny Hostin addressed claims she wasn't the holdout juror on a 1990s murder case, clarifying she held out on a different count than the man cited in the reporting did.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin addressed reporting about her identifying herself as a holdout juror in a gruesome murder case in the 1990s during the show's podcast Monday after resurfaced reports from multiple outlets said it was a man who was the holdout juror. "Someone on the internet dug up a Daily News article from 1991 that profiled another, different person that was a holdout juror. You were quoted in this article too, but they were talking about a man that other people pointed to as saying this is the reason we couldn't come to a verdict," Brian Teta, the producer of "The View," noted during the "Behind the Table" podcast. Hostin said she remembered him and explained that there were different counts in the case. ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW "So, as I recall, and look it up for yourselves, there were three counts, I believe. One was second-degree murder, but it was intentional. Then there was the defense to that was, we could consider the insanity defense, meaning that he committed the crime, but he was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease or defect. And there was a third count, or a third issue that we dealt with, and that issue was the desecration of Monika Beerle's remains," Hostin said. The co-host of "The View" said she felt strongly that he tried to hide the fact that he killed Beerle by dismembering her remains and that he should be found guilty of that count. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM "He was insane when he killed her," Hostin said. "And he said that, he confessed that he didn't realize that she was even dead. But then he decides to dismember her. I just thought that was so clear and gruesome and despicable to do that to someone's remains. I thought that he should be found guilty of that. And everyone else did too, except for this one guy. And we were, like, kind of looking at him, like, 'That was the easy one.' It was always the easy one. But we could not reach a unanimous verdict on that count." Teta noted that Hostin didn't mention this male juror on the show when she identified herself as the holdout juror in this trial. She clarified during the podcast that she was the holdout on a different count, the count related to the insanity defense. During the liberal talk show earlier this month, Hostin said she was a holdout juror on a case in which a man murdered his roommate and dismembered her. Hostin felt strongly that the man, Daniel Rakowitz, also known as "Butcher of Tompkins Square Park," was insane. The co-host shared an excerpt from a report in The New York Times about the trial, which was held in 1991. Rakowitz was acquitted by reason of insanity. Hostin, whose maiden name is Cummings and whose first name is Asunción, was quoted in a Feb. 23, 1991, New York Times report about the trial, which said, "Several jurors questioned afterward said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict." LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN "The View" co-host presented the article on the show while explaining the case. "That was me. It was because I saw clearly that he was psychotic," Hostin said during the show Sept. 22. After revealing she was the holdout juror on the case, the New York Post reported that other contemporaneous accounts identified an unemployed man as the principal holdout. The Post wrote that "Jurors told The Post, Newsday, the Daily News and the Associated Press that the actual holdout was an unemployed man who wanted to keep the trial going so he could continue getting paid by the court for his civic duty." "He was unemployed and liked the $15 a day and the three free meals," juror Valerie Holmes told Newsday after the verdict, according to contemporaneous coverage. CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR TAPS FORMER TRUMP LAWYER TO FIGHT BACK AS HE’S ‘DRAGGED THROUGH THE MUD’: ATTORNEY The Post also cited a law enforcement source familiar with the case who said, "We were told that the juror who held out was a man. There was no other description." Another factor, the New York Post said, was that "Hostin was quoted as a juror on the case in multiple news clips at the time, but she did not identify herself as the holdout, nor did any of the fellow jurors who talked to the press after the trial. Her statement to Newsday from the time even seemed to contradict her story." "Unfortunately for Sunny, one cannot simply put the toothpaste back in the tube. Hopefully, she's realized what kind of internet fervor she's created with this take that goes beyond her daily hare-brained political takes," Newsbusters Managing Editor Curtis Houck told Fox News Digital in a statement regarding Hostin's latest update on the story. "Rather, touting her juror status on such a gruesome case hopefully cuts across politics and into basic common sense. Her invocation of "shared experiences" is an utter crock. Bringing up a term from Woke 1 won't make her supposedly proud admission any less disturbing." Teta also asked Hostin to address what he described as the "lazy take," that she "got him out of jail, and she's proud of it," referring to criticism on the internet about her revelation. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "Why would I be proud of that?" Hostin asked. "It's an experience that I had that I shared so that people would understand better. I think our lived experiences are a very good way on this show, in particular, to explain to people, current events, right?" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The discussion started when the co-hosts weighed in on the holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy case. Clancy's defense attorney has criticized the holdout juror in the case.

articles.title: Australia replanted a former runway in the Daintree with 24,500 trees; the cleared land now reconnects a wildlife corridor
articles.summary: A former airstrip in the Daintree Rainforest is being restored to create safer, connected habitat for the Southern Cassowary.
articles.body: A former airstrip in the Daintree Rainforest is being restored to create safer, connected habitat for the Southern Cassowary. At Cow Bay, up to 10 hectares of barren land once stood between two sections of rainforest, disrupting an important wildlife corridor. A project led by Rainforest Rescue, with support from the Foundation for Australia’s Most Endangered Species (FAME), has focused on restoring the old runway with approximately 24,500 trees.Reportedly, the Southern Cassowary is listed as Endangered under Australia’s Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act and faces threats including habitat fragmentation, vehicle strikes and attacks by dogs. The restoration is designed to reconnect rainforest habitat while supporting the cassowary and many other rare, endangered and endemic species found in the Daintree Rainforest.How will 24,500 trees restore a former airstrip in the Daintree RainforestThe project focuses on the former airstrip property at Cow Bay, where an old runway has left up to ten hectares as a barren stretch between connected areas of rainforest. FAME describes the site as a key wildlife corridor in the Daintree Rainforest, with recent Southern Cassowary sightings in reforested areas.Restoring the remaining open section is intended to re-establish ecological continuity and create a continuous, safe and healthy habitat. Rainforest Rescue’s nursery and land management teams are cultivating and planting approximately 24,500 trees across the site. The planting is designed to reunite the two rainforest sections and support the Southern Cassowary as well as numerous rare and endangered species unique to the Daintree again.Why is the Southern Cassowary important to the rainforestThe Southern Cassowary is described as a keystone species of Australia’s rainforests and an indicator species whose well-being reflects the health of the ecosystem. It plays a key role in seed dispersal, helping promote forest regeneration and biodiversity. The species is listed as Endangered under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act.FAME lists habitat loss caused by development and fragmentation among its threats, along with vehicle strikes and attacks by domestic or feral dogs. Invasive species, including pigs and plants, can also degrade food sources and nesting areas.Cassowaries may also wander into settlements or agricultural zones, creating risks linked to human-wildlife conflict. Conservation efforts include habitat protection, reducing vehicle collisions, controlling invasive species, and public education.Which endangered species will benefit from the restored rainforest habitatRestoring the old runway is intended to benefit more than the Southern Cassowary. FAME says the project will support critically endangered fauna including the Beautiful Nursery-frog, Armoured Mistfrog and Northern Tinker Frog. Critically endangered flora listed include Crepidomanes aphlebioides, Hymenophyllum whitei, Thornton Peak Stink Bush and Bubbia whitean.Other listed beneficiaries include the Spectacled Flying-fox, northern Spotted-tailed Quoll, Eastern Curlew, Lesser Sand Plover, Red Goshawk, Tapping Nursery Frog, Waterfall Frog and Common Mistfrog.The project also includes endangered flora, endemic possums and gliders, endemic fauna and migratory birds. These include the Lemuroid Ringtail Possum, Green Ringtail Possum, Bennett’s Tree Kangaroo, Musky Rat Kangaroo, Daintree Rainbow Fish, Shining Starlings and Torresian Imperial-Pigeon naturally.How will the restored rainforest support waterways and wildlifeThe restoration has benefits beyond wildlife habitat. According to FAME, the new plantings will help naturally filter sediments from waterways, improving water quality and reducing turbidity for the Great Barrier Reef. The project is also intended to help mitigate climate change. Rainforest Rescue is increasing wildlife corridors and creating safe, connected habitats for rescued and restored wildlife across properties.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The common car seat mistakes experts often see and what they want you to do instead
articles.summary: A mom of three shares common car seat mistakes child passenger safety experts see, from loose harnesses to skipping the top tether. Plus, experts give advice on what to do instead.
articles.body: I’ve installed and reinstalled more than 15 car seats over the years for my three kids, ages 1, 2 and 4 years old. I still pull out the manual every time I switch a seat or move one to a different car. Car seats look simple until you’re actually buckling a squirming toddler into one at 7 a.m. And as it turns out, I’ve been getting small things wrong the whole time, right along with most other parents. “Kids grow fast, and sometimes you don’t realize how much they’ve grown until you’re buckling them in one morning and those straps suddenly look different,” says Michelle Pratt, CPST and founder of Safe in the Seat, a website dedicated to car seat safety. So I talked to three child passenger safety experts about this and the mistakes they see most, even from parents who are trying hard to get it right. They shared the small changes parents and caregivers could make to ensure that kids are strapped into car seats properly in order to avoid accidents and worse. The best car seats for infants and toddlers These picks held up against the same questions I ask before buying any seat: Does it fit my kid? Does it fit my car? Can I install it correctly every single time? To find these products I thoroughly researched them, digging through shopper reviews, Reddit threads and Facebook parenting groups and following Instagram chats for real-world takes. Then I went to stores like Bambi Baby or the Babylist Showroom to test seats in person before testing them with my kids. Car seats aren’t cheap, and I’ve learned the hard way that buying the wrong one the first time doesn’t save money, it just means buying another one a year later, so I’d rather spend more up front buying the right one the first time. Best car seat overall The Cybex is built to go the distance — literally. It’s been on more than 40 road trips since my son was born, adapting across both rear-facing and forward-facing setups so I’m not constantly rebuying as my kids grow. It feels sturdier than most seats I’ve installed, and it’s held up to years of daily use — snacks, spills, and all. It can stay installed rather than clicking in and out like an infant seat, and it’s a bigger price tag upfront, but for a seat we’ve used daily for years, it’s been worth it. Cybex recently released its Callisto T360 rotating car seat, an upgraded version of my beloved car seat. It’s officially the thing I’ll be gifting my closest family and friends when they have kids because I know they’ll have it for several years. Best infant car seat The newest Doona is a next-generation version of the classic Doona: lighter, with a new foot lock and a longer shade hood. It still clicks out of its base and rolls away on built-in wheels instantly, which meant more to me with my second kid than my first, once I actually understood the work that goes into getting a sleeping baby from the car to the pediatrician’s waiting room without a stroller. The catch: It’s infant-only, so you’ll likely outgrow it and need a new seat within a year. Best travel car seat The Wayb Pico folds down small enough to get through airport security with ease and use on the plane. It’s become my carpool go-to too — easy to toss in a trunk for a last-minute pickup. It’s pricier than most convertibles, with noticeably less padding, which my kids have never once complained about, though I notice every time I lift it. Best booster car seat Nuna’s AACE takes kids from a harnessed booster all the way to belt-positioning booster, so it’s lasted my eldest child years longer than I expected. It’s comfortable enough that our longer drives to see family don’t end in complaints (at least not about the seat), and it’s narrow enough that I’ve actually managed three-across in the back of our sedan — something I didn’t think was possible until I tried it. It costs a lot upfront, but it’s held up and stayed clean through years of use, and with a 120-pound weight limit, I haven’t had to rebuy. Best 360 car seat What are the most common car seat mistakes people make? Moving to the next stage too soon With my oldest son, I wanted to take him out of his rear-facing car seat when his legs started bending against the seat in front of him. But according to experts, kids should stay in each stage until they hit the seat’s height or weight limit, not until they seem too big for it, or hit a certain birthday. Data from the National Digital Car Seat Check Form (NDCF) found that nearly 87% of children were transitioned to an adult seat belt too soon in 2025, and 19.1% were moved to a booster seat too soon. The order should be: rear-facing until the seat’s rear-facing limit, then forward-facing with a harness and tether, then a booster until the vehicle’s own seat belt fits correctly on its own. This includes the transition from infant to toddler car seat. You get to decide when you’re done carrying an infant seat’s removable carrier. You don’t have to switch seats just because you’re tired of hauling it around. “If you’re over carrying it, leave it clicked into the base and use it like a stationary car seat, or move your baby into a rear-facing convertible seat,” says Pratt. “You’re still rear-facing. You’re just done carrying the carrier.”What to do: Look at the height and weight limits on the seat you’re actually using, don’t go by your kid’s age. The seat isn’t tight enough I’ve questioned more times than I can count whether the car seats my kids are in are actually secure. It always feels like I can wobble them. A seat can look installed correctly and still move too much. Grab it at the belt path and give it a firm shake. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) says it shouldn’t move more than an inch side to side or front to back. NDCF data shows installation is one of the most common problems technicians find: Nearly 70% of rear-facing car seats and just over 83% of forward-facing car seats were not used correctly in 2025. One rule I didn’t know about until I started reporting this: Don’t use the vehicle’s seat belt and the seat’s lower anchors, at the same time. Combining them doesn’t add extra protection, the two systems can pull against each other. “Crash-test data does not support using both restraints at once, so choose the method recommended for your seat and vehicle,” says Joshua Dilts, Certified Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST), and the lead car safety product manager at Chicco. What to do: Check for movement at the belt path, don’t test the seat from the top. *Any product recommendations in this story were made independently of Dilts, who we only consulted for guidance. We did not ask her for product recommendations. The harness isn’t as tight as you think it is I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve caught my kids’ harnesses slipping off their shoulders as we’re driving, or the chest strap sliding down toward their belly. To prevent this, try the pinch test: Buckle your child in, tighten the harness, then try to pinch the webbing at their shoulder. If you can grab a fold of it, it’s too loose. Harness height matters too. For rear-facing seats, straps should come from at or below the shoulders; for forward-facing seats, at or above. The chest clip belongs at armpit level. Check your manual, since it varies by seat. Fit isn’t a one-time check either. “Kids grow fast, and sometimes you don’t realize how much they’ve grown until you’re buckling them in one morning and those straps suddenly look different,” Pratt says. All three experts told me to do a quick check before every ride, and a closer one after a growth spurt or a jump in clothing size. What to do: Do the pinch test after buckling in your child, before you pull out of the driveway. You’re skipping the top tether I didn’t know this was a requirement until recently. It took two years of my son riding forward-facing before I understood the tether reduces movement in a crash. Once a seat is forward-facing, there’s a top tether in addition to the harness, and it’s easy to miss, since your child never sees it. NDCF data found that nearly 42% of forward-facing car seats did not use a tether when tether use was possible in 2025. “Many caregivers are unaware of its purpose or importance, even though it plays a critical role in reducing a child’s forward movement during a crash,” says Erica Tun, the Senior Director of Product for Child Restraint Systems (CRS) at Dorel Juvenile. What to do: If your child’s seat is forward-facing, check both the car seat and vehicle manuals to make sure you’re using the tether correctly. *Any product recommendations in this story were made independently of Tun, who we only consulted for guidance. We did not ask her for product recommendations. Your child’s winter coat is under the harness Winter is when I second guess myself the most: Do I dress my kids at home and strip off their coats in the car right before buckling them in, or leave the coats on for a five-minute drive? What if they overheat with it on, or get too cold without it? A bulky coat under the harness keeps the straps from sitting snugly against your child’s body. “You might tighten the harness and think you’ve got a great fit, but you’re really tightening it around all that puffiness,” Pratt says. What to do: Buckle your child in with a thin layer, tighten the harness properly, then add the coat backward or a blanket on top once they’re secured. There are a few products that make this easier. A Buckle Me Baby is designed to give kids winter-coat warmth without the bulk that interferes with harness fit, and a wraparound car seat cover, like the 7AM Helsinki or Benji Applique, zips on and off around the seat itself, so you can bundle your baby up right before you go and unzip them once they’re buckled in. If you’re not sure, have the seat checked. Getting a car seat checked by a certified child passenger safety technician is worth it anytime you buy a new seat, move your child to a new stage, or install a seat in a different car. Even experienced parents miss small details — I certainly have. NHTSA and Safe Kids Worldwide both have directories for finding certified technicians and car seat check events, and most local police and fire stations offer checks too. Remember that none of this means you’re doing everything wrong. It means car seats are complicated, kids grow fast, and the way you used a seat six months ago might not be right anymore. Take the extra few minutes to ensure you’re using it the way the manufacturer intended. Why are car seat mistakes so common? Nearly three-fourths (73.7%) of car seats checked by certified child passenger safety technicians in 2025 were incorrectly installed or used, according to the NDCF, a joint research effort from AAA, the National Safety Council and data collection company Westat. NHTSA estimates that correctly used child restraints cut fatality risk by 71% for infants and 54% for kids ages 1 to 4 years old. “The 71% figure is an effectiveness estimate, not a car seat usage rate,” Dilts told me. In other words, it’s the payoff for doing it right, not a measure of how many parents actually are. How to know whether a car seat is right for your child Before installation is even a consideration, there’s a shorter checklist that tells you whether a seat is the right fit at all: Does it fit your child? The minimum weight printed on the box doesn’t mean a seat fits every baby at that weight. Check the seat’s actual specs against your kid’s size, not just the headline range. Does it fit your car? The same seat that installs easily in a friend’s SUV might not work in your sedan’s back seat. Dilts recommends checking compatibility before you buy, especially if you’re dealing with a tight back seat or a three-across setup. Can you use it correctly every single time? “The best car seat is one that fits the child properly, fits the vehicle correctly, and can be used consistently and correctly on every ride,” Tun says. More features don’t help if they make the seat harder to install right. What does your family actually need? Do you want a car seat with stroller compatibility? Rotating designs? Three-across width or long-term convertibility? You’ll want to consider these features when shopping. Just remember, they’re all nice to have once fit and installation are covered, but they’re not a substitute for either. Meet our child passenger safety experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also aim to ensure that expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Joshua Dilts, certified child passenger safety technician (CPST), is the lead car safety product manager at Chicco. Any product recommendations in this story were made independently of Dilts, who we only consulted for guidance. We did not ask her for product recommendations. Erica Tun, is the Senior Director of Product for Child Restraint Systems (CRS) at Dorel Juvenile. Any product recommendations in this story were made independently of Tun, who we only consulted for guidance. We did not ask her for product recommendations. Michelle Pratt, CPST, is the founder of Safe in the Seat, a website dedicated to child car seat safety. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a mom who’s tested children’s gear through the most realistic daily scenarios: three kids under 5 years old and plenty of chaos. I’ve written about the products that make beach days with small kids easier, and the best no-screen travel toys my kids will actually play with. The products that make my lists solve real parenting problems. For this story, I talked to three child passenger safety experts about the mistakes they see most often with car seats, and tested more than 15 car seats across infant, convertible and all-in-one stages with my own three kids to see which held up to daily use. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
articles.summary: Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty of murder on Tuesday in the death of his wife, who was killed in their Ohio home in February.
articles.body: Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty of murder on Tuesday in the death of his wife, who was killed in their Ohio home in February. A jury took little over two hours to convict Flynn on all nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence. After the verdict was read by Judge Jeannine Pratt in the Miami County Court of Common Pleas in Troy, Ohio, Flynn broke down in tears and was repeatedly seen wiping his nose and eyes. He was taken from the courtroom in handcuffs. Sentencing will be on Oct. 5, where he faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Flynn, a former music pastor, told a 911 dispatcher that his wife, Ashley Flynn, who worked as a school teacher and volleyball coach, had been shot multiple times in the head by an intruder. He told the dispatcher that he did not know whether the intruder was still in their Tipp City home. In police interviews played in court, Flynn told officers that he was sleeping on the couch when he woke up to the sound of gunshots. He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.” When police arrived at the home on the day of the shooting, the garage door, a side door and the center console of Flynn’s pickup truck were open. Flynn told police that he kept a gun in the console, but no weapon was found there. Prosecutors alleged that Flynn, 40, staged the home invasion to mislead investigators and shared thoughts of killing his wife, 37, in text messages to his then-mistress. Authorities never found the gun used in the killing. “The evidence has proven the defendant’s account to be a complete fabrication,” Matthew C. Joseph, assistant prosecuting attorney for the Miami County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Troy, Ohio, said in closings Tuesday. “While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” Joseph said. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.” Joseph told the court that Flynn “wanted to be a victim” and wanted to “keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself.” “Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress,” Joseph said. “Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.” Over eight days, the jury heard from 40 prosecution witnesses, including Alleigha Botner, who said she met Flynn when she was 20 and an intern at his church. She said they had been having an affair at the time of Ashley’s killing. Botner, now 24, testified that Flynn had made remarks that he hated his wife and harbored thoughts of killing her. Botner sobbed on the stand as she read some of their text messages, telling the court that she regretted telling him in one message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.” Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.” In other text messages shown in court, Flynn discussed wanting his wife dead. “I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” he allegedly wrote in an August 2025 text, about six months before the killing. In another text, Botner said she wasn’t serious. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.” Botner told the court that her feelings about Flynn have since changed and she hated him. When a prosecutor asked her why, she said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.” The defense rested Monday without calling a single witness. Flynn’s attorney, Patrick Mulligan, said in his closing argument that being “unfaithful doesn’t equal murder.” “This case is wholly lacking in concrete evidence. Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case,” he said. Flynn sang in the televised auditions in Chicago for Season 12 of “American Idol” in 2013 but did not advance to the main competition.

articles.body:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

In truth, once it became clear that the military remote-controlled robots that were used found no explosives in the vans, only petrol, the investigation inevitably changed.

It left detectives with five men from London in their 20s in police custody who had simply been found parked up near the air base in the middle of the night in suspicious circumstances and with some petrol - but little other usable concrete evidence.

It might have been hard to persuade a senior officer or a magistrate to extend the suspects' detention without something more definite.

The men were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE), not the Terrorism Act (TACT). This meant detectives had the option to use police bail with strict conditions, but could not hold the men for 14 days, which they could have done if TACT had been used.

What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe

More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford

For a while it was unclear whether the men were already being watched by undercover surveillance teams when they were spotted by villagers in the dead of night, or whether the villagers really were the first people to alert the police.

Taylor has now given some assistance on this, saying the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received", suggesting the police had some other intelligence

Certainly security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days, so certainly there had been some intelligence about a possible attack. Elite firearms officers were very quick to respond to the villagers' 999 calls.

Both counter-terrorism and military sources have told me that this story is still quite near the beginning, raising the possibility that detectives are trying to identify some kind of "controlling hand" behind the presence of the suspects in Whelford with their petrol.

The men could be entirely innocent and able to give a good explanation for being in Whelford on Sunday

They could have been paid or tricked into moving the vehicles and the petrol, but unaware of who they were working for

Or they could have been part of a plot which was interrupted before it reached a more dangerous phase

That is why the next bit of the counter-terrorism investigation is so vital.

By examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses, and using the covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence, detectives are trying to build a clearer picture.

On that critical investigation rests the decision over whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five men, and whether we ever find out the true story of the mysterious RAF Fairford plot.

articles.title: Texas ‘lionesses’ win major prison air-conditioning fight after years of documenting extreme heat; court orders all prisons cooled by 2029, with 88,697 people lacking AC
articles.summary: They call themselves “lionesses” for a reason.
articles.body: They call themselves “lionesses” for a reason. The women behind the Lioness Justice Impacted Women’s Alliance say their name reflects the determination, loyalty and collective strength that have driven their fight for safer conditions inside Texas prisons.Founded in 2022 by a small group of formerly incarcerated women, the nonprofit has spent years pushing back against practices they say harm people caught in the criminal legal system. One of its biggest battles has been over extreme temperatures inside Texas prisons.Now, a federal court has ordered the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) to air-condition all state prisons by December 31, 2029.The 19th reported that the ruling followed a lawsuit brought by Lioness alongside Texas Prisons Community Advocates and Texas Citizens United for Rehabilitation of Errants. U.S. District Judge Robert Pitman found that the conditions violated the Eighth Amendment’s protection against cruel and unusual punishment.Nearly 89,000 people were in unair-conditioned unitsIn his 150-page order, Pitman wrote that approximately 88,697 incarcerated people were housed in units without air conditioning heading into summer 2026.Only about 37% of the TDCJ population had access to what the agency calls “cool beds.”The judge pointed to the extreme temperatures prisoners face during Texas summers, noting that outdoor heat indexes can rise above 130 degrees.Pitman wrote that incarcerated people in the state were “suffering, and in some cases dying, in extreme heat every summer.”The ruling sets a December 31, 2029 deadline for the state to complete the air-conditioning work. TDCJ must provide progress reports to the court every six months, and Texas plans to appeal.‘I don’t know if I will survive this’For Marci Marie Simmons, Lioness’ director of communications, the ruling is personal.Simmons spent 10 years incarcerated in a Texas prison and remembers what it was like to endure summer heat inside concrete and steel buildings.“I remember laying in my bunk — we weren’t allowed to lay on the floor in that prison — and I remember thinking, ‘I don’t know if I will survive this,’” Simmons said.After the ruling, Simmons said Lioness staff were celebrating while also preparing for the next stage of the fight.“We’ve been laughing and crying and celebrating, and also, you know, preparing because we know that this is just one step in the fight,” she said.The organisation has only one full-time executive director and four part-time employees, all of whom are formerly incarcerated. Yet its network has expanded to about 500 members, including around 400 people currently behind bars.The group advocates for the health, safety and well-being of nearly 20,000 women and transgender people held in Texas prisons and jails.Letters from inside became evidenceFor years, Lioness received letters from incarcerated people describing what extreme heat felt like inside their units.Some wrote because they were physically suffering. Others, according to Diane Thompson, Lioness’ director of member relations, simply wanted someone outside the prison walls to know what they were experiencing.“They needed somebody on the outside to hear them and to know what they were living through,” Thompson wrote.Thompson kept detailed records of the correspondence, documenting the names and units of incarcerated members, the dates of their letters, the problems they reported and other relevant details.She also kept the original letters.The correspondence later became part of the legal record, with Pitman referring to the letters multiple times in his ruling.“We are a membership-based organization. We include our incarcerated members in our decision-making. They lead our advocacy work,” Simmons said. “Because of the structure of our organization, that is what got us to the finish line in this case.”Prison heat can worsen existing health problemsThe consequences of extreme heat can be particularly serious for incarcerated people who already have medical conditions.Carlee Purdum, an associate professor of sociology at the University of Houston who studies the effects of disasters on incarcerated populations, said the psychological impact can be as significant as the physical one.“The most significant impact is just the helplessness and the dehumanization that a person feels,” she said.People participating in Purdum’s surveys reported heat illness, fainting, seizures and rashes.Wanda Bertram, a spokesperson for the Prison Policy Initiative, also noted that certain medications can increase vulnerability to prolonged heat exposure.People with high blood pressure, diabetes and heart conditions can face additional risks, she said.Women in particular can experience additional health challenges. Federal data show that a majority of incarcerated women have chronic medical conditions, while women are more likely than men to report serious psychological distress.Purdum’s focus groups with women from Lioness also brought up pregnancy, menopause and the difficulties of managing those experiences in extreme heat.Extreme heat during pregnancy has been associated with higher risks of preeclampsia, premature birth and low birth weight.Meanwhile, the number of older women in state and federal prisons has increased sharply. Women over 50 accounted for 18% of the prison population in 2023, compared with 8% in 2008.Cooling down can depend on prison officialsFor people currently incarcerated, the court-ordered changes will not happen overnight.Purdum said people inside prisons have limited control over their own environment. If they run out of water, they may have to ask prison staff for more. Access to cooled areas can also require permission.“People in the free world just do not understand what it means to not be able to take the simplest actions to stay comfortable, to stay alive,” she said.Texas is also not alone in facing questions about prison temperatures. A 2019 Prison Policy Initiative report found that at least 13 states did not require universal air conditioning in prisons, with many of those states in the South.“A lot of places in the country have extreme heat, even more so now with global warming,” Bertram said. “There aren’t really states in the country where this isn’t an issue.”‘Lionesses stick together’For the women behind Lioness, however, the fight has never been only about air conditioning.It has been about people who remain inside and who, they say, have often felt forgotten.“Our organization is named Lioness, and there’s a reason for that. We move like the animal. Lionesses stick together; they stay together,” Simmons said.She said that collective determination helped the organisation take on what she described as one of the largest prison systems in the country.Purdum has seen that same solidarity among women inside Texas prisons.During focus groups, women described checking on elderly prisoners and those with medical conditions, sharing water and redirecting their own resources to help others endure extreme heat.“They were just these kinds of extraordinary examples of care,” Purdum said. “We have a lot to learn from them.”For her, that solidarity also explains why the legal victory carries significance beyond the courtroom.“It was always about the people that they still had on the inside, and they never stopped fighting for them,” Purdum said. “That was extraordinary to just witness. I’m just very proud to have had the opportunity to work with them.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn found guilty of murdering wife
articles.summary: Caleb Flynn weeps in court as he is convicted of shooting his wife, Ashley, dead in their Ohio home.
articles.body:
A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been found guilty of murdering his wife.

Caleb Flynn, 40, fatally shot Ashley Flynn twice in the back of the head while she slept at their Ohio home on 16 February this year, then tried to claim that intruders had shot her.

Flynn wept in court as the jury delivered its verdict after deliberating for less than three hours.

He also was found guilty of the other eight charges against him, which included aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. He faces life in prison without parole.

Closing arguments ended on Tuesday in Flynn's trial after eight days of testimony, which included a song played in court that prosecutors say he wrote and dedicated to the woman with whom he was having an affair.

Throughout the trial, the prosecution presented evidence including police body camera footage, and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch around the time of the murder, which took place in Tipp City, a suburb of Dayton.

They also called dozens of witnesses, including his former mistress Alleigha Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church.

Some of their 100,000 exchanged text messages were read aloud in court. The defence called no witnesses.

"I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail," Flynn wrote in a message to Botner, 24, in August 2025.

In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone."

Testifying in court, Botner said she now hates Flynn "because I believe that he murdered his wife".

During closing arguments on Tuesday, prosecuting attorney Paul Watkins leaned heavily into Flynn's text exchanges, which he said demonstrated the defendant's "hatred" for his wife.

He described Flynn as being afraid to lose custody of his daughters in a divorce, as well as his job with his wife's family business and his job at the church.

An emotional Flynn was seen in court at times sniffling and wiping tears from his eyes.

Watkins also said that when police arrived at the family home in the early hours on 16 February, Flynn told police he had been in his daughters' bedroom when he heard gunfire.

Flynn said he found his 37-year-old wife dead in the bedroom, after noticing the garage side door was open. Watkins said Flynn later told investigators he had not been to the garage, contradicting his earlier statement.

Flynn's defence lawyer Patrick Mulligan, meanwhile, told the court there was no concrete evidence, saying: "Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case."

Mulligan said the issue was not whether Flynn was a good husband to his wife, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach, and that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder.

"They can't find the gun, therefore they blame it on him?" Mulligan questioned, referring to the charge of tampering with evidence that Flynn also faced.

Flynn's gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open.

Earlier in the trial, Botner took the stand as a witness for two days, offering testimony about her nearly 18-month relationship with Flynn.

In addition to reading some of their text exchanges, she also explained the lyrics line by line from an AI-generated song.

Video of the jury's reaction to the song, including what looked like laughter, went viral.

Prosecutors also called Joseph Wilhelm, a special agent from Ohio's Bureau of Criminal Investigations, as a witness.

He said multiple apps were uninstalled from Flynn's phone before his wife's death, including Instagram and an AI-music generating app.

The music-generating app, Wilhelm said, "related to his relationship with Alleigha Botner".

Flynn appeared in 2013 on the 12th series of American Idol, and sang before judges Mariah Carey, Nicki Minaj and Randy Jackson.

He was featured in televised auditions, and was given a "golden ticket" to go to Hollywood, but he never reached the main competition.

"Music is all I know, it's what I live to do and I love to sing, so that's why I auditioned," he said in videos shown on the programme.

"Maybe my wife kinda nudged me a little, too."
